blocks.html: Economics starts from a plain fact: people want more than the world can make. Hours in the day, farmland, workers, machines and oil are all limited, while new wants appear as soon as old ones are met. That gap between wants and resources is called scarcity. It is the reason every person, family, business and country has to choose.

Scarcity means wants are greater than the resources available to satisfy them. Economists sort resources into four factors of production: land (every natural resource), labor (human effort and skill), capital (tools, machines and buildings made to produce other things) and entrepreneurship (organizing the other three and taking the risk of a new venture).

Scarcity is a gap, not poverty. A billionaire still has 24 hours in a day and must choose how to spend them; a rich country still has to decide whether a hillside becomes a park or a housing development. Because each resource has other possible uses, putting it to one use means it is not available for another. That is why scarcity forces choices, and why the next idea in this course, the cost of a choice, follows from it.

cards.text: The oven in a pizza shop
cards.why: An oven is a tool built to make other things (pizzas): capital.

cards.text: Iron ore still in the ground
cards.why: Natural resources count as land, wherever they are found.

cards.text: A nurse’s hours at the hospital
cards.why: Human effort and skill is labor.

cards.text: Fish in a lake that a fishing crew harvests
cards.why: Fish in the wild are a natural resource: land.

cards.text: The founder who risks her savings to open a food truck
cards.why: Combining resources and bearing the risk is entrepreneurship.

cards.text: A delivery van owned by a bakery
cards.why: The van is used to produce a service (delivery): capital.

cards.text: A programmer writing an app
cards.why: The programmer’s work is labor.

cards.text: A warehouse building
cards.why: A building made to produce or store goods is capital.

blocks.cap: Sort each resource into a factor of production, then press Check. The note on each wrong card says why.

blocks.title: The resources behind a slice of pizza
blocks.q: A pizza shop uses flour from wheat, a pizza oven, two cooks, the owner who started the shop and plans the menu, and the land the shop stands on. Sort these into the four factors of production.
steps: Natural resources are land: the plot the shop stands on, and the wheat field the flour came from.
Human work is labor: the two cooks.
Things made to produce other things are capital: the oven (and the shop's building, counters and mixers).
The person who brings it all together and takes the risk is the entrepreneur: the owner.
blocks.a: Land: the plot and the wheat field. Labor: the cooks. Capital: the oven. Entrepreneurship: the owner.

blocks.html: Calling money "capital." In everyday talk, a business's money in the bank is its capital. In economics, capital means the physical tools, machines and buildings used to make goods and services. Money buys resources, but money itself doesn't bake a pizza. A second mix-up: scarcity is not the same as a shortage or as poverty. A shortage happens in one market at one price; scarcity is always present, even for the richest society. Quick check: ask "could this thing be used to produce something?" A van, yes; a bank balance, no.

You'll also meet the term human capital: the knowledge and skills workers gain from schooling, training and experience. It makes labor more productive. In the four-factor list it belongs with labor, because it lives in the worker.

blocks.html: Because resources are scarce (Scarcity and the Factors of Production), choosing one thing always means not choosing something else. Economists measure the cost of a choice by what you give up to make it.

The opportunity cost of a choice is the value of the next best alternative you give up. It counts money you pay and anything else you sacrifice, such as your time or the wage you could have earned. Only the single best alternative counts, not every alternative added together.

Why only the best alternative? With the same evening or the same \$20 you could have done only one other thing. If you hadn't gone to the game, you would have picked the best option left on your list, not all of them at once. So the real sacrifice is that one best option. And why does time count? Because an hour spent one way can't be sold or used another way. When an hour could have earned \$15 at a job, spending it elsewhere costs \$15, even though no money changes hands.

blocks.name: ec-sort

cards.text: Tuition for the year
cards.why: You pay it only if you go to college.

cards.text: Textbooks
cards.why: You buy them only because you are in school.

cards.text: The pay from a full-time job you turn down
cards.why: Giving up earnings is the largest cost of college for many students.

cards.text: Food you would eat either way
cards.why: You eat whether or not you go to school, so the choice does not change it.

cards.text: Rent you would pay either way
cards.why: If you would rent the same place anyway, choosing college does not add it.

cards.text: The fee you paid last year for a campus visit
cards.why: Money already spent cannot be recovered by any choice now: it is a sunk cost.

blocks.cap: What does a year of full-time college cost? Sort each item. Count only what changes because of the choice.

blocks.title: Saturday choices
blocks.q: On Saturday afternoon Jen can work a 5-hour shift at \$14 an hour, babysit for \$50, or go to a free street festival. She goes to the festival. What is her opportunity cost?
steps: List the alternatives she gives up and their values: the shift is worth $5 \times \$14 = \$70$; babysitting is worth \$50.
She could have done only one of them. The best one is the shift, worth \$70.
The festival is free, so there is nothing else to add.
blocks.a: \$70, the value of the best alternative (not \$70 + \$50 = \$120).

blocks.title: A concert that costs time and money
blocks.q: Omar buys a \$40 concert ticket. The concert and travel take 3 hours, which he could have spent working at \$12 an hour. What is the opportunity cost of going?
steps: Money given up: the \$40 ticket, which he could have spent on something else.
Time given up: 3 hours of work, worth $3 \times \$12 = \$36$.

blocks.html: Two mistakes are common. Adding up every alternative: in Jen's case \$120, as if she could have worked and babysat in the same hours. And leaving out costs that aren't paid in money, such as time or a forgone wage: then Omar's concert looks like it costs only \$40. Studies find that even trained economists sometimes miss forgone earnings. Check: ask "what would I actually have done instead?" and count that one option, money and time together.

blocks.html: Economics studies how people deal with scarcity (Scarcity and the Factors of Production). When economists speak, they sometimes describe how the economy works and sometimes say what they think should be done. Telling the two apart is the first step to a fair argument.

A positive statement describes how the world is, was or will be. It can be tested against evidence, at least in principle, and it stays positive even if it turns out to be false. A normative statement says what ought to be. It rests on values and often uses words like should, ought, better, fair or too much.

The split matters because the two kinds of disagreement are settled differently. If two people disagree about whether a soda tax cuts soda sales, data can settle it: that is a positive question. If they agree on the facts but disagree about whether the tax is worth it, evidence can inform them but not settle it, because they weigh goals (health, freedom of choice, the burden on low-income buyers) differently. That is why economists who agree on the facts can still disagree about policy.

blocks.name: ec-sort

cards.text: When the price of gasoline rises, people buy less of it.
cards.why: It describes behavior that data can check.

cards.text: Gasoline taxes are too high.
cards.why: "Too high" is a judgment about values.

cards.text: A rent ceiling below the market rate causes a shortage of apartments.
cards.why: A testable prediction about cause and effect.

cards.text: The city should spend more on parks.
cards.why: "Should" signals a value judgment.

cards.text: Raising the minimum wage to 30 dollars an hour would end all poverty.
cards.why: Almost surely false, but it is a claim about facts that evidence can test, so it is positive.

cards.text: The top income tax rate ought to be 50 percent.
cards.why: A number does not make it positive: "ought" makes it a recommendation.

blocks.cap: Sort each statement, then press Check. Two cards are set as traps.

blocks.title: Three statements
blocks.q: Classify each: (a) "College graduates earn more on average than people with only a high school diploma." (b) "Reducing unemployment is more important than reducing inflation." (c) "Printing money always lowers prices."
steps: (a) Can data check it? Yes, with earnings surveys. Positive.
(b) "More important" ranks goals; no data set can say which goal matters more. Normative.
(c) This one is false (printing a lot of money tends to raise prices), but it makes a claim that evidence can test. Positive.

blocks.html: Calling a statement normative because you disagree with it, or positive because it sounds scientific or has numbers in it. "The tax rate on the highest earners should be 50 percent" is normative even though it has a number; "a \$30 minimum wage would end all poverty" is positive even though it is wrong. Check: ask "could evidence, at least in principle, prove this false?" If yes, it is positive. If it needs a judgment about what is good or fair, it is normative.

Throughout this course you'll see the same split. Where economists broadly agree on a positive question (for example, that a binding price ceiling causes a shortage), lessons say so. Where they disagree on facts that are still being studied, or on the values behind a policy, lessons lay out each side.

blocks.html: Every choice has an opportunity cost (Opportunity Cost), and a whole society makes millions of choices a day. Every society has to answer three questions: what to produce, how to produce it, and for whom. Economic systems are different ways of answering them.

In a market economy, households and firms answer the three questions through buying and selling, guided by prices and profits. In a command economy, government planners decide. In a traditional economy, custom and habit decide. Every real economy is mixed: markets and government both play a part, in different balances.

How can a market answer "what to produce" with no one in charge? Prices carry information and incentives. When more people want a good, its price rises; that tells sellers people value it more and rewards them for making more. A planner has to gather the same information from millions of people and firms, which is hard to do quickly. But markets also leave some jobs undone or done badly: roads, national defense, pollution and help for people with little income come up later in this course. So the real question in every country is where to draw the line, and that is debated.

blocks.name: ec-sort

cards.text: A bakery adds a new bagel after customers line up for it.
cards.why: Buyers’ spending and the chance of profit decided what to make.

cards.text: A planning ministry sets how many tractors each factory must build.
cards.why: A government plan decides what and how much.

cards.text: Fishing grounds pass from parent to child, and the catch is shared by custom.
cards.why: Custom decides who works where and who gets what.

cards.text: Wages rise for nurses when hospitals compete to hire them.
cards.why: A price (the wage) rations a scarce skill.

cards.text: The state assigns graduates to jobs.
cards.why: Planners, not a labor market, decide how labor is used.

cards.text: Children learn their parents’ trade, as their parents did.
cards.why: Tradition answers "how" and "who."

blocks.cap: Which kind of decision is each? Real countries mix all three.

blocks.title: Who answers the question?
blocks.q: In Country A, most prices are set by buyers and sellers, but the government runs schools and courts, taxes income and pays pensions. In Country B, a central plan sets output targets, but families may sell vegetables from their own plots at whatever price they can get. How would you describe each?
steps: Country A relies mainly on markets, with an important government role: a mixed economy that leans toward markets.
Country B relies mainly on planning, with a small market: a mixed economy that leans toward command.
Neither is "pure"; they differ in the balance.
blocks.a: Both are mixed: A leans market, B leans command.

blocks.html: Picturing a real country as a pure market or a pure command economy. No modern economy is either: even the most market-based ones have public schools, courts, regulations and taxes, and even heavily planned economies have had private plots and informal markets. Check: when you classify a country, ask how much of each question is answered by prices and how much by government, and expect "some of both."

Economists broadly agree that prices coordinate most everyday goods well, and that some goods and problems need government. How large government's role should be is a normative question, and people answer it differently.

blocks.html: Opportunity cost (Opportunity Cost) is easiest to see with money. If you have a fixed budget and two things to buy, every combination you can afford in full lies on one line, and that line is an equation in Standard Form and Intercepts.

With income $I$ and prices $P_x$ and $P_y$, the bundles that spend the whole budget satisfy $$P_x\,x + P_y\,y = I.$$ The intercepts are $I/P_x$ (all on $x$) and $I/P_y$ (all on $y$). With $y$ on the vertical axis the slope is $-P_x/P_y$: each extra unit of $x$ costs $P_x/P_y$ units of $y$. That ratio is the opportunity cost of $x$.

Solve the budget equation for $y$: $$y = \frac{I}{P_y} - \frac{P_x}{P_y}\,x.$$ The vertical intercept $I/P_y$ is what you can buy if you spend everything on $y$. Buying one more unit of $x$ uses $P_x$ dollars, and those dollars would have bought $P_x/P_y$ units of $y$. So the slope is a price ratio, and it measures what one good costs in units of the other.

blocks.name: ec-choice
blocks.cap: A \$60 budget with burgers at \$6 and movies at \$12. Drag the bundle: on the line you spend exactly \$60; inside, money is left; outside, the bundle costs too much.

blocks.title: Intercepts and slope
blocks.q: Lia has \$60 for burgers (\$6 each) and movie tickets (\$12 each). Find both intercepts and the opportunity cost of one burger.
steps: All burgers: $60/6 = 10$ burgers. All movies: $60/12 = 5$ movies.
The line runs from $(0, 5)$ to $(10, 0)$. Slope $= \dfrac{0 - 5}{10 - 0} = -\dfrac{1}{2}$.
One burger costs \$6, half the price of a movie, so it costs $\tfrac{1}{2}$ movie.
blocks.a: Intercepts 10 burgers and 5 movies; one burger costs $\tfrac{1}{2}$ movie.

blocks.title: Can she afford it?
blocks.q: With the same budget, is 4 burgers and 3 movies affordable? What about 6 burgers and 3 movies?
steps: $4(\$6) + 3(\$12) = \$24 + \$36 = \$60$: exactly the budget, a point on the line.
$6(\$6) + 3(\$12) = \$36 + \$36 = \$72 > \$60$: outside the line, not affordable.
blocks.a: The first is affordable (on the line); the second is not.

blocks.html: Putting the wrong intercept on an axis, such as $I/P_y$ on the $x$-axis, or flipping the ratio and saying a burger costs 2 movies. Check an intercept by multiplying back: 10 burgers $\times$ \$6 = \$60. Check the ratio with common sense: the cheaper good must cost less than one unit of the pricier good.
If the price of one good changes, the line pivots around the other good's intercept. If income changes, the whole line shifts in parallel, because the price ratio, and so the slope, stays the same.

blocks.html: A whole economy faces the same kind of tradeoff as a shopper with a budget, only with workers and machines instead of dollars. You know opportunity cost from Opportunity Cost, and you know how to read the story a graph tells from Describing Graphs in Words. Put them together and you get the production possibilities curve (PPC).

A PPC shows the largest combinations of two goods an economy can produce when it uses all its resources with today's technology. A point on the curve is efficient. A point inside is possible but inefficient: some resources are idle or misused. A point outside is unattainable for now.

On the curve, every worker and machine is busy, so the only way to get more robots is to move some of them away from wheat: more of one means less of the other. Inside the curve, some workers or machines sit idle (as in a recession), so the economy could have more of both goods just by using them. Outside the curve, there aren't enough resources, or good enough technology, to make that much, although growth may make it possible later.

blocks.name: ec-ppc
blocks.cap: Drag the point. Inside the curve it is possible but wasteful; on it, efficient; outside, out of reach for now. "Put idle resources to work" moves an inside point toward the curve.

head: Point
Robots
Wheat (tons)
blocks.cap: A production possibilities table: each row is one point on the curve.

blocks.title: Reading points against the table
blocks.q: Using the table, classify each combination: (a) 20 robots and 60 tons of wheat; (b) 30 robots and 60 tons of wheat; (c) 10 robots and 90 tons of wheat.
steps: (a) With 20 robots the economy can make at most 75 tons (point C). 60 is less than 75: inside, inefficient.
(b) With 30 robots the most is 50 tons (point D). 60 is more than 50: outside, unattainable for now.
(c) Exactly point B: on the curve, efficient.

blocks.html: Calling a point inside the curve "impossible." It is perfectly possible; it is just wasteful, because the same resources could make more. Another mix-up: thinking the PPC shows what people want. It shows only what the economy can make. Which point on the curve a society picks depends on what people want, but their wants don't move the curve. Check: for a given amount of the horizontal good, read the most the curve allows of the other, then compare.
A PPC holds three things fixed: the amount of resources, the technology, and the time period. Change one of them and the whole curve moves, which is the subject of Growth and Shifts of the PPC.

blocks.html: On a PPC (The Production Possibilities Curve) more of one good means less of the other. How much less is the opportunity cost, and you can read it off the graph as a slope, the idea from Slope as Rate of Change.

Moving along a PPC, the opportunity cost of the extra units of $x$ is the amount of $y$ given up. Per unit: $$\text{opportunity cost of one } x = \frac{\text{amount of } y \text{ given up}}{\text{amount of } x \text{ gained}},$$ the size of the slope. A straight PPC has a constant opportunity cost. A PPC bowed out from the origin has an increasing opportunity cost.

Why does the curve bow out? Resources are not equally good at everything. When a farm country starts making robots, it first moves the people and land least useful for farming, so little wheat is lost. As it makes more robots, it has to move its best farmland and most skilled farmers, so each extra batch of robots costs more wheat. If resources were equally suited to both goods, every step would cost the same and the PPC would be a straight line.

blocks.name: ec-ppc
blocks.cap: Each step adds 10 robots (blue) and costs wheat (red). The red drops grow, 10, 15, 25, 50 tons, so the opportunity cost rises.

blocks.title: A straight-line PPC
blocks.q: A country can make either 40 robots or 120 tons of wheat, or any combination on the straight line between. What is the opportunity cost of one robot? Of one ton of wheat?
steps: Moving from all wheat to all robots gains 40 robots and gives up 120 tons.
One robot costs $\dfrac{120}{40} = 3$ tons of wheat.
One ton of wheat costs $\dfrac{40}{120} = \dfrac{1}{3}$ robot, the reciprocal.
blocks.a: 3 tons of wheat per robot; $\tfrac{1}{3}$ robot per ton of wheat.

blocks.title: Rising cost along a table
blocks.q: Using the table in the picture, find the opportunity cost per robot of moving from 10 to 20 robots, and from 20 to 30 robots.
steps: From 10 to 20 robots, wheat falls from 90 to 75: 15 tons for 10 robots, or $\dfrac{15}{10} = 1.5$ tons per robot.
From 20 to 30 robots, wheat falls from 75 to 50: 25 tons for 10 robots, or $2.5$ tons per robot.
The cost per robot rises as more robots are made: increasing opportunity cost.
blocks.a: 1.5 tons per robot, then 2.5 tons per robot.

blocks.html: Two errors are common: reporting what was gained instead of what was given up, and flipping the ratio, as in "a robot costs $\tfrac{1}{3}$ ton" when it costs 3. Check with units: the cost of a robot is measured in wheat, so wheat goes on top: tons of wheat per robot. And the two costs must be reciprocals of each other.

blocks.html: A PPC is drawn for fixed resources and technology (Opportunity Cost Along the PPC). Over time those change, and so does the curve. The question to ask about any event: does it change what the economy can make, or only how much of it is being used?

The PPC shifts outward (economic growth) when the economy gains resources, such as more workers, more capital or newly found natural resources, or better technology. It shifts inward when resources are lost, as in a disaster. Technology that helps only one good moves only that good's end of the curve. Putting idle resources back to work moves a point from inside the curve toward it; the curve itself stays put.

The curve answers "what is the most we could make with everything we have and know?" More workers or machines, or a better way of making things, raise that maximum, so the curve moves out. Unemployed workers going back to work don't change the maximum; they were already counted as part of what the economy could use. So a recovery from a recession moves the economy's point, while growth moves the curve.

blocks.name: ec-ppc
blocks.cap: A new technology for robots moves only the robot end of the curve. The point starts inside: press "Put idle resources to work" to see a recovery, which is a different thing.

blocks.title: Curve or point?
blocks.q: For a country making robots and wheat, what happens to its PPC or its position in each case? (a) A recession ends and laid-off factory workers are rehired. (b) Better education raises the skills of the whole workforce. (c) A new seed raises wheat output per acre, with no change in robot making.
steps: (a) The workers were already part of the economy's resources; they were idle. The point moves from inside toward the curve; the curve does not shift.
(b) Workers can produce more of both goods: the whole curve shifts outward.
(c) Only wheat production improves: the curve's wheat end moves out; the robot intercept stays.
blocks.a: (a) point moves toward the curve; (b) whole curve out; (c) wheat end out only.

blocks.html: Shifting the whole curve out when idle workers go back to work. That is a move from inside the curve toward it, not growth. Check: ask "does the economy now have more resources, or better technology, than before?" If it is only using more of what it already had, the curve doesn't move.

Choosing today matters for tomorrow. An economy that puts more of its resources into capital goods (machines, factories, training) instead of goods to consume now gives up some consumption today, but its PPC tends to shift out faster later.

blocks.html: Two producers can each draw a PPC and measure their own opportunity costs (Opportunity Cost Along the PPC). Comparing those costs, as Unit Rates compares prices per item, tells us who should make what.

A producer has an absolute advantage in a good if it can make more of it with the same resources (or the same amount with fewer). A producer has a comparative advantage in a good if its opportunity cost of making it is lower. Unless two producers have identical opportunity costs, each has a comparative advantage in something.

Why must each have a comparative advantage in something? Opportunity costs come in reciprocal pairs. If Ana gives up $\tfrac{1}{2}$ shirt per loaf, then a shirt costs her 2 loaves. If Ben gives up 1 shirt per loaf, a shirt costs him 1 loaf. Ana's loaf is cheaper, so Ben's shirt must be: when one cost is lower, its reciprocal is higher. Being faster at everything (absolute advantage) can't change that.

blocks.name: ec-trade
blocks.cap: Ana can make 6 loaves or 3 shirts a day; Ben 4 loaves or 4 shirts. The table of opportunity costs shows who gives up less for each good.

blocks.title: An output table
blocks.q: In a day Ana can bake 6 loaves of bread or sew 3 shirts; Ben can bake 4 loaves or sew 4 shirts. Who has the absolute advantage in each good, and who has the comparative advantage?
steps: Absolute advantage: Ana makes more bread (6 > 4); Ben makes more shirts (4 > 3).
Ana's cost of a loaf: $\dfrac{3 \text{ shirts}}{6 \text{ loaves}} = \dfrac{1}{2}$ shirt. Ben's: $\dfrac{4}{4} = 1$ shirt. Ana's is lower, so Ana has the comparative advantage in bread.
Ana's cost of a shirt: $\dfrac{6}{3} = 2$ loaves. Ben's: $\dfrac{4}{4} = 1$ loaf. Ben has the comparative advantage in shirts.
blocks.a: Ana: bread (both absolute and comparative). Ben: shirts (both).

blocks.title: An input table: hours per unit
blocks.q: Country X needs 2 hours of labor per bushel of corn and 6 hours per bike. Country Y needs 4 hours per bushel and 8 hours per bike. Who has the comparative advantage in bikes?
steps: Here smaller numbers are better: fewer hours per unit. X has the absolute advantage in both goods.
In X, 6 hours spent on one bike could have made $6 \div 2 = 3$ bushels: a bike costs 3 bushels.
In Y, 8 hours on one bike could have made $8 \div 4 = 2$ bushels: a bike costs 2 bushels.
Y gives up less corn per bike, so Y has the comparative advantage in bikes (and X in corn).

blocks.html: Confusing the two kinds of advantage, and treating the bigger number as better in an input table. In the second example X is faster at both goods, yet Y has the comparative advantage in bikes. Check: in an input table, first ask "how many of the other good could these same hours have made?" Then compare those opportunity costs; the lower one wins.

blocks.html: Once you know who has the comparative advantage in each good (Absolute and Comparative Advantage), the next question is what happens if each specializes and they trade. The surprising answer: both can end up with more than they could make on their own.

When each producer specializes in its comparative-advantage good and they trade, total output rises, and both can consume beyond their own PPC. The terms of trade (the price of one good in units of the other) must lie between the two producers' opportunity costs; then each gets the other good for less than it would cost to make it.

Take Ana and Ben from the last lesson. A loaf costs Ana $\tfrac{1}{2}$ shirt to make and costs Ben 1 shirt. If they trade at $\tfrac{3}{4}$ shirt per loaf, Ana gets $\tfrac{3}{4}$ shirt for a loaf that cost her only $\tfrac{1}{2}$ shirt to make, and Ben gets a loaf for $\tfrac{3}{4}$ shirt instead of the 1 shirt it would cost him. Each gains $\tfrac{1}{4}$ shirt per loaf. At terms below $\tfrac{1}{2}$, Ana would rather make shirts herself; above 1, Ben would rather bake. Inside the band, both gain.

blocks.name: ec-trade
blocks.cap: Ana bakes, Ben sews, and they trade 2 loaves for 1.5 shirts. Both consumption points land outside their own PPCs. Try terms outside the band of 0.5 to 1.

blocks.title: Total output before and after
blocks.q: Before trade, Ana splits her day: 3 loaves and 1.5 shirts. Ben splits his: 2 loaves and 2 shirts. What happens to total output if Ana makes only bread and Ben only shirts?
steps: Before: $3 + 2 = 5$ loaves and $1.5 + 2 = 3.5$ shirts.
After: Ana makes 6 loaves; Ben makes 4 shirts.
Total output rises by 1 loaf and 0.5 shirt, with the same work.
blocks.a: From 5 loaves and 3.5 shirts to 6 loaves and 4 shirts.

blocks.title: Does the deal work for both?
blocks.q: Ana and Ben specialize and trade 2 loaves for 1.5 shirts ($\tfrac{3}{4}$ shirt per loaf). What does each consume?
steps: Ana keeps $6 - 2 = 4$ loaves and gets 1.5 shirts. On her own, 4 loaves would leave time for only 1 shirt: she is outside her PPC.
Ben keeps $4 - 1.5 = 2.5$ shirts and gets 2 loaves. On his own, 2 loaves leave time for only 2 shirts: he is outside his PPC too.
blocks.a: Ana: 4 loaves and 1.5 shirts. Ben: 2 loaves and 2.5 shirts. Both are better off.

blocks.html: Thinking trade is a contest where one side's gain is the other's loss, or that a producer who is better at everything has nothing to gain. Ana is better at bread and Ben at shirts here, but even when one side has the absolute advantage in both goods, both gain as long as their opportunity costs differ. Check any proposed deal: is each side's consumption point outside its own PPC?

Economists broadly agree that trade raises total output and income. They also agree the gains are not shared evenly: workers and firms that compete with imports can lose, sometimes for years. How much to help them, and how, is debated. Trade at the World Price measures the winners and losers in one market.

blocks.html: Most choices are not all-or-nothing. You rarely decide whether to study, but how many more hours; a café doesn't decide whether to open, but whether to stay open one more hour. The cost of each extra step is an opportunity cost (Opportunity Cost), and economists weigh it one unit at a time: "at the margin."

Marginal benefit (MB) is the extra benefit from one more unit; marginal cost (MC) is the extra cost. Keep going while $MB \ge MC$ and stop before the first unit with $MB < MC$. That quantity makes net benefit (total benefit minus total cost) as large as possible. A sunk cost, money already spent that can't be recovered, should not change the choice.

Net benefit changes by $MB - MC$ with each unit. While a unit adds more benefit than cost, net benefit rises; once a unit adds less, net benefit falls. So net benefit peaks at the last unit with $MB \ge MC$. Sunk costs drop out for the same reason: the money is gone whichever way you choose, so it lowers every option's net benefit by the same amount, and can't change which option is best.

And letting a sunk cost drive the choice: "we already paid for the tickets, so we have to go." Research on decisions finds people do often fall for this. blocks.html: Economists use the same one-more-unit thinking (Marginal Benefit, Marginal Cost and Sunk Costs) to describe the benefit people get from buying things. They call that benefit utility, measured in made-up units called utils.

Total utility (TU) is the satisfaction from all the units you consume. Marginal utility (MU) is the extra satisfaction from one more unit: $MU = \Delta TU$. The law of diminishing marginal utility: as you consume more of a good in a period, each extra unit usually adds less than the one before. Total utility rises as long as MU is positive, peaks where MU reaches zero, and falls only if MU turns negative.

The first slice of pizza meets your most urgent want, hunger. The second still tastes good, but you're less hungry; by the fifth, you're nearly full. Each unit serves a less pressing want, so it adds less. Total utility is the running sum of the marginal utilities: adding a smaller positive number still makes the total bigger. Only adding a negative MU (the slice that makes you feel sick) makes the total fall.

blocks.name: ec-marginal
blocks.cap: Total utility climbs while each bar of marginal utility is above zero, even as the bars shrink. The sixth slice has negative MU, and total utility falls.

blocks.title: From totals to marginals
blocks.q: Total utility from slices of pizza is 20, 34, 44, 50, 52 and 50 utils for 1 to 6 slices. Find the marginal utility of each slice. Where is total utility highest?
steps: MU falls from the start, but TU keeps rising through slice 5, because each MU is still positive. TU is highest at 5 slices.
blocks.a: MU: 20, 14, 10, 6, 2, −2. Total utility is highest at 5 slices.

blocks.html: Thinking total utility falls as soon as marginal utility falls. From slice 1 to slice 5, MU drops every time, yet TU rises every time. A smaller gain is still a gain. Check: TU falls only when an MU is negative.
No one can measure satisfaction in utils. The numbers are a way to describe how people rank choices, and the conclusions in this unit depend only on that ranking: which option adds more.

blocks.html: You know marginal utility (Total and Marginal Utility) and the budget line (Budget Constraints). Put them together and you can answer a shopper's real question: with a fixed budget, how much of each good gives the most total utility? The key is a unit rate, utility per dollar, like the price per ounce in Unit Rates.

Spend each next dollar where it adds the most utility: on the good with the higher marginal utility per dollar, $MU/P$. When the budget is spent, the best bundle satisfies $$\frac{MU_x}{P_x} = \frac{MU_y}{P_y}.$$

Suppose the last dollar on pizza gives 6 utils and the last dollar on books gives 4. Move one dollar from books to pizza: you lose about 4 utils and gain about 6, so total utility rises. As you buy more pizza its MU falls, and as you buy fewer books their MU rises, so the two ratios move toward each other. Only when they are equal does no swap help. This also explains the law of demand: if the price of pizza rises, $MU/P$ for pizza falls, and the rule says buy less of it.

blocks.html: The utility rule (Marginal Utility per Dollar) says a shopper buys a good until its marginal utility per dollar matches other goods'. Raise the good's price and its utility per dollar falls, so the shopper buys less. Add up every shopper and you get demand. Its graph is a line or curve, read the way you read Linear Models in Context.

The law of demand: other things equal, when the price of a good rises, the quantity demanded falls, and when the price falls, it rises. Demand is the whole relationship between price and quantity demanded: a demand schedule (a table) or a demand curve (its graph, with price on the vertical axis). Market demand adds every buyer's quantity at each price.

Three forces push the same way. Utility per dollar: at a higher price, the good gives less satisfaction per dollar, so buyers move their spending elsewhere. Substitution: buyers switch to alternatives that are now relatively cheaper. Income: a higher price leaves less buying power for everything. "Other things equal" (economists also say ceteris paribus) matters: the law describes what happens when only the price changes.

blocks.name: ec-market
blocks.cap: Drag the point along the demand curve: a lower price, a larger quantity demanded. The curve itself stays where it is.

blocks.title: A demand schedule from an equation
blocks.q: Demand for tacos at a food truck is $Q_d = 120 - 10P$ per day, with $P$ in dollars. Find the quantity demanded at \$3, \$5 and \$7.
steps: Each \$1 rise in price lowers quantity demanded by 10: the law of demand.

blocks.title: Market demand
blocks.q: At a price of \$4, Ana wants 3 tacos, Ben wants 5 and Cy wants 0. At \$2, they want 5, 8 and 2. Find the market quantity demanded at each price.
steps: Add across buyers at the same price.

blocks.html: Using "demand" for one number, the amount people buy. Demand is the whole schedule. When the price changes, demand does not change; the quantity demanded does, as you slide along the same curve. Check: if your sentence names one price and one quantity, the word you want is "quantity demanded."

Why is price on the vertical axis, when it is the cause? It is a tradition from the economist Alfred Marshall, and every textbook keeps it. Read a demand curve sideways: pick a price on the vertical axis, go across to the curve, then down to the quantity.

blocks.html: A demand curve can be written two ways, and textbooks, exams and later courses use both. Switching between them is the skill from Solving for a Variable: solve for the other letter. You met the first form in The Law of Demand.

$$Q_d = a - bP \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad P = \frac{a}{b} - \frac{1}{b}\,Q.$$ The quantity intercept is $a$ (the quantity demanded at a price of zero). The price intercept is $a/b$ (the price at which no one buys, sometimes called the choke price). With price on the vertical axis, the slope of the graph is $-\dfrac{1}{b}$, not $-b$.

Start from $Q = a - bP$. Add $bP$ and subtract $Q$: $bP = a - Q$. Divide by $b$: $P = \dfrac{a}{b} - \dfrac{Q}{b}$. That is the line as the graph draws it, with $P$ up and $Q$ across, so its slope is the coefficient of $Q$, $-\tfrac{1}{b}$. The number $b$ says how many units of quantity are lost per \$1 of price; its reciprocal says how many dollars of price per unit of quantity.

blocks.name: ec-market
blocks.cap: Each curve is labeled in both forms. Demand $Q_d = 20 - 2P$ is the same line as $P = 10 - Q/2$: it meets the axes at 20 units and \$10.

blocks.title: From quantity form to price form
blocks.q: Demand is $Q_d = 20 - 2P$. Find the price intercept, the quantity intercept, the slope of the graph and the inverse form.
steps: Quantity intercept: set $P = 0$: $Q = 20$.
Price intercept: set $Q = 0$: $0 = 20 - 2P$, so $P = 10$.
Solve for $P$: $2P = 20 - Q$, so $P = 10 - \tfrac{1}{2}Q$.
Slope with $P$ on the vertical axis: $\dfrac{0 - 10}{20 - 0} = -\dfrac{1}{2}$.

blocks.title: From price form to quantity form
blocks.q: Inverse demand is $P = 12 - 0.5Q$. Write it as $Q_d$ in terms of $P$, and find the quantity demanded at \$8.
steps: Add $0.5Q$ and subtract $P$: $0.5Q = 12 - P$.
Multiply by 2: $Q_d = 24 - 2P$.
At \$8: $Q_d = 24 - 16 = 8$. Check in the price form: $12 - 0.5(8) = 8$. ✓

blocks.html: Taking the $-2$ in $Q = 20 - 2P$ as the slope of the graph, or swapping the intercepts. If you learned $y = mx + b$, it is natural to read $Q$ as $y$, but on these graphs price is "$y$." Check: plot both intercepts, $(20, 0)$ and $(0, 10)$, and compute rise over run: $-10/20 = -\tfrac{1}{2}$.

blocks.html: A demand curve (The Law of Demand) answers one question: how much would buyers want at each price, with everything else held fixed? So there are two different ways buying plans can change, and economists use two different names for them.

A change in the good's own price causes a change in quantity demanded: a movement along the demand curve. A change in anything else that affects buyers (income, tastes, prices of related goods, expectations, the number of buyers) causes a change in demand: the whole curve shifts. An increase in demand shifts the curve right; a decrease shifts it left.

The curve is drawn with the good's own price on an axis, so a change in that price is already "on the map": you move to a different point on the same curve. Income, tastes and the rest are not on either axis. When one of them changes, buyers want a different amount at every price, so every point moves, and that is a new curve.

blocks.name: ec-market
blocks.cap: Left: the price changes, and buyers slide along the same curve (a change in quantity demanded). Right: income changes, and the whole curve moves (a change in demand).

blocks.title: Four headlines about coffee
blocks.q: Classify each: (a) the price of coffee falls; (b) a study links coffee to longer life; (c) incomes fall, and coffee is a normal good; (d) the price of coffee rises.
steps: (a) Own price: a movement along the curve, an increase in quantity demanded.
(b) Tastes: buyers want more at every price, an increase in demand (shift right).
(c) Income: buyers want less at every price, a decrease in demand (shift left).
(d) Own price: a decrease in quantity demanded, a movement up along the curve.
blocks.a: (a) and (d) are movements; (b) and (c) are shifts.

blocks.html: Saying "the price fell, so demand increased." A lower price raises the quantity demanded; demand, the whole curve, is unchanged. Mixing the two leads to the "double shift" error later. Check: ask "is the thing that changed this good's own price?" If yes, it is a movement; if no, it is a shift.

blocks.html: A shift of demand comes from something other than the good's own price (Change in Demand vs Change in Quantity Demanded). Economists keep a short list of what those things are.

Demand shifts when buyers' tastes, incomes, expectations (about future prices or incomes) or numbers change, or when prices of related goods change (the next lesson). For a normal good, higher income raises demand; for an inferior good, higher income lowers it. "Inferior" is a technical word for goods people buy less of as they get richer, not a judgment of quality.

Each item changes how much buyers want at every price. With more income, people can afford more of most things, so demand for normal goods rises. But with more income some people also switch away from goods they bought to save money, such as long-distance bus trips instead of flying, or store brands instead of name brands; for those buyers, those goods are inferior. Expectations work through timing: if buyers expect the price to rise next month, they buy more now, so today's demand rises.

blocks.name: ec-market
blocks.cap: Try the demand buttons. Each moves the whole demand curve. The supply curve stays put, and the price change moves sellers along it.

blocks.title: Which way does demand shift?
blocks.q: What happens to demand for each good? (a) Movie tickets in a city whose population grows. (b) Store-brand cereal when incomes rise, for buyers who see it as inferior. (c) Gasoline today when drivers expect a big price rise next week.
steps: (a) More buyers: demand increases, a shift right.
(b) Inferior for these buyers: higher income, demand decreases, a shift left.
(c) Buy now before the rise: today's demand increases.

blocks.html: Assuming more income raises demand for every good. It does for normal goods, and lowers it for inferior ones. And the same good can be normal for one buyer and inferior for another. Check: ask "when these buyers get richer, do they buy more of this, or trade it for something they like better?"
One trap: a change in the good's own expected price shifts today's demand, but a change in the good's current price never does. The expected future price is not on the axis; today's price is.

blocks.html: The last demand shifter on the list (What Shifts Demand) is the price of a related good. It is the one that most often trips people up, because one price change touches two markets.

Two goods are substitutes if a higher price for one raises demand for the other (coffee and tea). They are complements if a higher price for one lowers demand for the other (coffee and coffee filters). The good whose price changed has a movement along its own demand curve; the related good's demand curve shifts.

Substitutes do the same job, so when coffee gets pricier some buyers switch to tea: tea is wanted more at every tea price. Complements are used together, so pricier coffee makes the coffee-and-filter pair more expensive; people drink less coffee and need fewer filters at every filter price. In both cases, the coffee market itself only sees a change in its own price: a movement along coffee's demand curve.

blocks.name: ec-market

determinants.label: Price of a substitute rises
determinants.why: Some buyers switch to this good from the pricier substitute

determinants.label: Price of a complement rises
determinants.why: The pair costs more to use together, so buyers want less of this good at every price

blocks.cap: This is the market for tea, the related good. A pricier substitute (coffee) shifts tea demand right; a pricier complement (say, honey) shifts it left.

blocks.title: One price change, two markets
blocks.q: The price of coffee rises sharply. What happens to (a) the quantity of coffee demanded, (b) the demand for tea, (c) the demand for coffee filters?
steps: (a) Coffee's own price rose: quantity demanded of coffee falls, a movement along coffee's demand curve.
(b) Tea is a substitute: demand for tea increases (shifts right).
(c) Filters are a complement: demand for filters decreases (shifts left).

blocks.title: Name the relationship
blocks.q: When the price of gaming consoles fell, sales of video games rose. Are consoles and games substitutes or complements?
steps: A lower console price raised demand for games.
The price of one and the demand for the other moved in opposite directions: complements.

blocks.html: Shifting the demand curve of the good whose own price changed: "coffee got more expensive, so coffee demand shifts left." The coffee market moves along its curve; it's the other good's curve that shifts. Check: write down which market you are drawing. A price on that graph's own axis moves you along; a price from another market shifts the curve.

blocks.html: Now the other side of the market. Sellers decide how much to offer by comparing price with the extra cost of making more, the same marginal thinking as in Marginal Benefit, Marginal Cost and Sunk Costs. Supply equations work like the demand equations in Demand Equations Both Ways.

The law of supply: other things equal, a higher price brings a larger quantity supplied. Supply is the whole relationship, a schedule or an upward-sloping curve, often written $Q_s = c + dP$. A change in the good's own price moves sellers along the supply curve; anything else that changes their plans shifts it.

Making more usually costs more per extra unit: a bakery has to pay overtime, run older ovens or buy flour on short notice. That rising marginal cost means sellers will make an extra unit only if the price covers it. A higher price covers more of those costlier units, so firms supply more, and new sellers find it worth joining in. So quantity supplied rises with price.

blocks.name: ec-market
blocks.cap: Drag the price line up the supply curve: at each higher price, sellers offer more. The curve is $Q_s = -4 + 2P$: no one sells below \$2.

blocks.title: A supply schedule
blocks.q: Supply is $Q_s = -4 + 2P$. Find the quantity supplied at \$5 and at \$8, and the lowest price at which anyone sells.
steps: Below \$2 the formula gives a negative quantity, which means nothing is offered.

blocks.title: Market supply
blocks.q: Three farms would sell 10, 6 and 0 crates of peaches at \$3, and 16, 12 and 4 crates at \$5. Find the market quantity supplied at each price.
steps: Add across sellers at the same price.

blocks.html: Saying a higher price "increases supply." A higher price increases the quantity supplied, a movement along the curve; supply, the whole curve, hasn't moved. Check, as with demand: is the change the good's own price? Then it's a movement.

blocks.html: Supply shifts when something other than the good's own price changes sellers' plans (The Law of Supply), just as demand shifts in Change in Demand vs Change in Quantity Demanded.

Supply shifts when input prices, technology, taxes or subsidies on the producer, the prices of other goods the seller could make, sellers' expectations, the number of sellers, or natural conditions such as weather change. An increase in supply shifts the curve right: more offered at every price. A cost increase is a decrease in supply: the curve shifts left (which looks like up).

Most shifters work through cost. If flour gets pricier, every loaf costs more to make, so at each price bakers offer fewer loaves: the curve moves left. Seen the other way, the bakers now need a higher price for each quantity: the same curve moves up. Up and left are one move. Technology does the reverse: lower cost per unit, more offered at each price, a shift right (or down). More sellers add their quantities at every price, so market supply moves right.

blocks.name: ec-market
blocks.cap: Try "Input prices rise": the supply curve moves up and to the left, a decrease in supply. "New technology" moves it down and to the right, an increase.

blocks.title: Increase or decrease?
blocks.q: For the supply of bread, classify: (a) the price of wheat rises; (b) a new oven bakes twice as fast; (c) bakers expect bread prices to be much higher next month; (d) three new bakeries open.
steps: (a) Input cost up: supply decreases (left).
(b) Better technology: supply increases (right).
(c) Sellers hold some back to sell later at the higher price: today's supply decreases.
(d) More sellers: supply increases.

blocks.html: Reading the upward move after a cost increase as "more supply." On the graph the curve rises, but higher means sellers want more money for each quantity, so they offer less at each price: a decrease. Check: at a fixed price, look across. Is the new curve to the left of the old one? Then supply decreased.

blocks.html: Put demand and supply on one graph. Where they cross, buyers' and sellers' plans match. Finding that point with equations is the skill from Variables on Both Sides: set the two quantities equal. You know supply from The Law of Supply.

The equilibrium price $P^*$ is the price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied; that common amount is the equilibrium quantity $Q^*$. For $Q_d = a - bP$ and $Q_s = c + dP$: $$a - bP = c + dP \;\Rightarrow\; P^* = \frac{a - c}{b + d}, \qquad Q^* = a - bP^*.$$

At any other price, the plans don't match, and someone has a reason to change the price. Above $P^*$, sellers offer more than buyers want, unsold goods pile up and sellers cut prices. Below $P^*$, buyers want more than is offered, they bid prices up, and sellers raise them. Only at $P^*$ does nobody have that reason. That is what "equilibrium" means: a resting point.

blocks.name: ec-market
blocks.cap: Drag the price line. Away from \$6 there is a gap between quantity demanded and quantity supplied, and the arrow shows which way the price is pushed.

blocks.title: Solve for the equilibrium
blocks.q: $Q_d = 20 - 2P$ and $Q_s = -4 + 2P$. Find the equilibrium price and quantity.
steps: Set them equal: $20 - 2P = -4 + 2P$.
Add $2P$ and 4 to both sides: $24 = 4P$, so $P^* = 6$.
Quantity: $Q_d = 20 - 2(6) = 8$. Check with supply: $-4 + 2(6) = 8$. ✓

blocks.title: Inverse forms
blocks.q: Demand is $P = 15 - Q$ and supply is $P = 3 + 0.5Q$. Find the equilibrium.
steps: Here each equation gives a price, so set the prices equal: $15 - Q = 3 + 0.5Q$.

blocks.html: Equilibrium doesn't mean everyone is happy with the price; it means no one has a reason to change it. Real markets take time to get there, and they keep moving because the curves keep shifting, which is the subject of the next lessons.

Solving $Q_d = Q_s$ for the price and then reporting that number as the quantity, or plugging the price into only one equation. In the first example, $P = 6$ but $Q = 8$. Check: put $P^*$ into both equations; they must give the same quantity, and that quantity is $Q^*$.

blocks.html: Equilibrium (Market Equilibrium) is where plans match. At any other price there is a gap, and the gap has a name.

At a price below equilibrium, quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied: a shortage of $Q_d - Q_s$. Buyers compete and the price tends to rise. At a price above equilibrium, quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded: a surplus of $Q_s - Q_d$. Sellers cut prices and the price tends to fall.

A low price does two things at once: it makes buyers want more (along demand) and sellers offer less (along supply), so the gap opens from both sides. As the price rises, buyers drop out and sellers offer more, closing the gap from both sides until it is gone at $P^*$. A high price works the same way in reverse.

blocks.name: ec-market
blocks.cap: At \$4, buyers want 12 but sellers offer 4: a shortage of 8. Drag the price above \$6 to see a surplus.

blocks.title: Below equilibrium
blocks.q: With $Q_d = 20 - 2P$ and $Q_s = -4 + 2P$, what happens at a price of \$4?
steps: Buyers want more than is offered: a shortage of $12 - 4 = 8$ units.
The price tends to rise toward \$6.
blocks.a: A shortage of 8; the price is pushed up.

blocks.title: Above equilibrium
blocks.q: Same market, price \$9.
steps: A surplus of $14 - 2 = 12$ units; sellers cut prices toward \$6.
blocks.a: A surplus of 12; the price is pushed down.

blocks.html: You can see these gaps in daily life. Shortages show up as lines, waiting lists and empty shelves; surpluses as piles of unsold goods and clearance sales. When a law keeps the price from moving, the gap lasts: that is the subject of Price Ceilings and Price Floors.

Confusing a shortage with scarcity, or thinking a surplus pushes the price up. Scarcity is always there; a shortage exists only at a price below equilibrium, and goes away when the price rises. A surplus means unsold goods, so the pressure is down. Check: compare the price with $P^*$. Below means shortage and up; above means surplus and down.

blocks.html: Now let one curve move. You can tell which curve and which way (What Shifts Supply, Substitutes and Complements), and you know a gap pushes the price (Shortages and Surpluses). Put the pieces together in four steps.

(1) Start at the equilibrium. (2) Decide which curve the event shifts. (3) Decide which way. (4) Find the new crossing. Demand up: $P$ and $Q$ both rise. Demand down: both fall. Supply up: $P$ falls and $Q$ rises. Supply down: $P$ rises and $Q$ falls.

Take an increase in demand. At the old price, buyers now want more than sellers offer: a shortage. The price rises, and as it rises, sellers move up along the supply curve, offering more. The new equilibrium has a higher price and a higher quantity. The supply curve never moved; the higher price only moved sellers along it.

blocks.name: ec-market
blocks.cap: Step through a demand increase: the shift, the shortage at the old price, then the new equilibrium at a higher price and quantity. Supply stays put.

blocks.title: A bad harvest
blocks.q: A freeze destroys part of the orange crop. What happens to the price and quantity of oranges?
steps: The freeze affects sellers' ability to produce: supply shifts.
Fewer oranges at every price: supply decreases (left).
At the old price there is now a shortage, so the price rises, and buyers move up along demand, buying less.

blocks.title: With numbers
blocks.q: $Q_d = 20 - 2P$ and $Q_s = -4 + 2P$. Incomes rise and demand increases by 6 units at every price. Find the new equilibrium.
steps: New demand: $Q_d = 26 - 2P$.
$Q = 26 - 2(7.5) = 11$. Both rose, from \$6 and 8 units.

blocks.html: "Double shifting": the price rises, so supply increases, so the price falls… The higher price moves sellers along the supply curve; it doesn't shift it. A price is never a shifter in its own market. Check: name the one event and the one curve it shifts. Everything else that happens is a movement along the curve that did not shift.

blocks.html: Sometimes two things happen at once: a new technology arrives just as incomes rise. Each shift alone has a clear effect (When One Curve Shifts). Together, one result is certain and the other is not.

When both curves shift, one of price or quantity changes in a definite direction and the other is ambiguous: it depends on which shift is larger. Demand and supply both up: $Q$ rises, $P$ ambiguous. Both down: $Q$ falls, $P$ ambiguous. Demand up and supply down: $P$ rises, $Q$ ambiguous. Demand down and supply up: $P$ falls, $Q$ ambiguous.

Work each shift alone, then combine. A demand increase pushes $P$ up and $Q$ up. A supply increase pushes $P$ down and $Q$ up. On quantity they agree, so $Q$ surely rises. On price they disagree, so the result depends on the sizes: a big demand shift and a small supply shift raise $P$; the reverse lowers it; equal-sized pushes can leave it unchanged. A quick way: make a two-row table of arrows and look for the column where the arrows agree.

blocks.name: ec-market
blocks.cap: Demand and supply both increase. Quantity rises for sure; the gold band shows the range the price could land in, depending on the sizes of the shifts.

head: Event

blocks.title: Smartphones
blocks.q: Incomes rise (smartphones are a normal good) while a cheaper chip lowers production costs. What happens to the price and quantity of smartphones?
steps: Higher income: demand increases, which on its own raises both the price and the quantity.
Cheaper chip: supply increases, which on its own lowers the price and raises the quantity.
Quantity: both push it up, so it rises. Price: one pushes up and one down, so it is ambiguous.
blocks.a: Quantity rises; the price change is ambiguous.

blocks.title: With numbers, the ambiguity resolves
blocks.q: $Q_d = 20 - 2P$ and $Q_s = -4 + 2P$. Demand increases by 6 and supply increases by 2. Find the new price and quantity.
steps: New curves: $Q_d = 26 - 2P$ and $Q_s = -2 + 2P$.
Here demand's shift was larger, so the price rose. With a supply shift of 10 instead, the price would have fallen.

blocks.html: Giving a definite answer for the ambiguous variable, such as "the price rises" in the smartphone case. Without the sizes of the shifts, you can't tell. Check: write the arrows for each shift separately; if they disagree, the honest answer is "it depends on which shift is larger."

blocks.html: The law of demand (The Law of Demand) says quantity demanded falls when price rises. Elasticity says by how much, in a way that doesn't depend on units. It is built from percent changes, which you know from Percent Increase and Decrease.

The price elasticity of demand is $$E_d = \left|\frac{\%\Delta Q_d}{\%\Delta P}\right|.$$ In this course we report it as a positive number. Use the midpoint method: divide each change by the average of the two values. Demand is elastic if $E_d > 1$, inelastic if $E_d < 1$ and unit elastic if $E_d = 1$.

Why percents? A slope depends on units: a price change of 1 dollar is 100 cents, and a quantity in pounds is 16 times bigger in ounces. Percent changes have no units, so elasticity can compare gasoline with movie tickets. Why the midpoint? A plain percent change depends on the direction: going from 4 to 6 is a 50% rise, but from 6 to 4 is a 33% fall. Dividing by the average, 5, gives 40% either way, so the elasticity between two points is the same in both directions. The ratio is negative for demand (price and quantity move opposite ways), so we drop the sign and remember it.

blocks.name: ec-elasticity
blocks.cap: Drag points A and B along the demand line. The midpoint calculation is written out below the graph. Notice that the elasticity changes as you move the pair along the line, even though the slope never does.

blocks.title: An elastic stretch
blocks.q: When a café raises the price of a muffin from \$4 to \$6, the number sold falls from 100 to 60 a day. Find the price elasticity of demand.
steps: $E_d = \left|\dfrac{-50\%}{40\%}\right| = 1.25$. Greater than 1: elastic.

blocks.title: An inelastic stretch
blocks.q: When the price of a commuter train ticket rises from \$2 to \$3, daily riders fall from 110 to 90 (in hundreds). Find the elasticity.
steps: $E_d = \dfrac{20\%}{40\%} = 0.5$: inelastic. Riders have few alternatives for getting to work.

blocks.html: Three slips are common: dividing the percent change in price by the percent change in quantity (upside down), using the slope $\Delta Q/\Delta P$ instead of percent changes, and dividing the two changes by different bases (one by the old value, the other by the average). Check: quantity goes on top ("how much does quantity respond?"), and every percent change uses the midpoint of its own two values.
A quick use: if $E_d = 2$, a 5% price rise cuts quantity demanded by about $2 \times 5\% = 10\%$.

blocks.html: With the number in hand (Price Elasticity of Demand), the next question is why some goods have elastic demand and others inelastic. The answer comes back to substitutes (Substitutes and Complements).

Demand is more elastic when there are close substitutes, when the good is a luxury rather than a necessity, when it takes a large share of the budget, when buyers have more time to adjust, and when the market is narrowly defined (one brand of cereal rather than food). Elasticity is not the slope: along a straight-line demand curve, demand is elastic at high prices and inelastic at low prices.

All five come back to one question: how easily can buyers do without? With good substitutes, a price rise sends buyers elsewhere. A luxury can be skipped; insulin can't. A 10% rise in rent hurts more than a 10% rise in salt, so people search harder for alternatives. Over time, people find new options: buy a smaller car, move closer to work. As for the line: high on a demand curve, quantity is small, so a few units lost is a big percent; price is large, so a \$1 change is a small percent. The ratio is big. Low on the line, the reverse holds.

blocks.name: ec-elasticity
blocks.cap: The same straight line is elastic on its upper half and inelastic on its lower half, with unit elasticity exactly at the midpoint. Drag the pair of points down the line and watch the number fall.

blocks.title: Which is more elastic?
blocks.q: For each pair, which has the more elastic demand? (a) Gasoline over one week, or over five years. (b) One brand of bottled water, or water in general. (c) Insulin, or concert tickets.
steps: (a) Five years: there is time to buy a more efficient car, carpool or move.
(b) One brand: other brands are close substitutes.
(c) Concert tickets: a luxury with many alternatives; insulin is a necessity with no close substitute.
blocks.a: Gasoline over five years; one brand of water; concert tickets.

blocks.title: Two points on one line
blocks.q: Demand is $Q_d = 20 - 2P$. Is demand elastic or inelastic between \$8 and \$9? Between \$2 and \$3?
steps: \$8 to \$9: quantities 4 and 2. $\%\Delta Q = \tfrac{2}{3} \approx 67\%$; $\%\Delta P = \tfrac{1}{8.5} \approx 12\%$. $E_d \approx 5.7$: elastic.
\$2 to \$3: quantities 16 and 14. $\%\Delta Q = \tfrac{2}{15} \approx 13\%$; $\%\Delta P = \tfrac{1}{2.5} = 40\%$. $E_d \approx 0.33$: inelastic.
Same slope, very different elasticities.
blocks.a: Elastic near the top (about 5.7); inelastic near the bottom (about 0.33).

blocks.html: Judging elasticity by how steep a graph looks. Steepness depends on the units on the axes, and on a straight line the elasticity changes from point to point even though the slope never does. Check: compute percent changes, or remember the rule of thumb for a straight line: above the midpoint elastic, below it inelastic.

blocks.html: A seller cares about elasticity (Elastic, Inelastic and What Decides It) because it decides what a price change does to revenue. Total revenue is what buyers spend: $TR = P \times Q$.

If demand is elastic, a higher price lowers total revenue and a lower price raises it. If demand is inelastic, a higher price raises total revenue. If demand is unit elastic, revenue doesn't change. On a straight-line demand curve, total revenue is largest at the midpoint, where demand is unit elastic.

A price rise has two effects on revenue: each unit sold brings in more (the price effect), but fewer units are sold (the quantity effect). In percent terms, $\%\Delta TR \approx \%\Delta P + \%\Delta Q$. When demand is elastic, the quantity falls by a bigger percent than the price rises, so revenue falls. When it is inelastic, the price effect wins. At unit elasticity they cancel, which is why revenue peaks there.

blocks.name: ec-elasticity
blocks.cap: The gold rectangle is total revenue, $P \times Q$, at point A. The lower panel plots revenue against quantity: it rises through the elastic stretch, peaks at the midpoint (10 units, \$5) and falls through the inelastic stretch.

blocks.title: The test with numbers
blocks.q: A theater raises ticket prices from \$10 to \$12, and attendance falls from 500 to 450. Is demand elastic or inelastic in this range?
steps: Price rose and revenue rose: demand is inelastic.
Check with the midpoint method: $\%\Delta Q = 50/475 \approx 10.5\%$, $\%\Delta P = 2/11 \approx 18.2\%$, $E_d \approx 0.58 < 1$. ✓

blocks.title: The revenue-maximizing price
blocks.q: Demand is $Q_d = 100 - 5P$. What price maximizes total revenue, and what is that revenue?
steps: The demand line runs from \$20 (where $Q = 0$) down to 100 units (where $P = 0$).
Revenue peaks at the midpoint: $P = \$10$, $Q = 100 - 50 = 50$.

blocks.html: Believing a price increase always raises revenue because each unit brings in more money. That ignores the units no longer sold. In the elastic stretch, raising the price loses so many sales that revenue falls. Check: compute $P \times Q$ before and after.

This is why a business with inelastic demand can raise revenue with a price rise, while one facing close competitors usually cannot. Profit also depends on costs, which come later in the course; revenue alone doesn't decide the best price.

blocks.html: Elasticity works on the sellers' side too. The calculation is the midpoint method from Price Elasticity of Demand, applied to the supply curve from The Law of Supply.

The price elasticity of supply is $$E_s = \frac{\%\Delta Q_s}{\%\Delta P},$$ a positive number because quantity supplied rises with price. Supply is more elastic when firms have more time, spare capacity, inputs that are easy to get, or goods they can store. Perfectly inelastic supply is a vertical line ($E_s = 0$); perfectly elastic supply is horizontal.

Supply elasticity measures how easily sellers can make more when the price rises. A bakery with idle ovens can bake more by tomorrow; a vineyard can't grow more grapes until it plants vines and waits years. That's why supply is usually more elastic in the long run than in the short run. At the extreme, the number of seats in a stadium on game night can't change at all, whatever the price: the supply curve is vertical.

blocks.name: ec-elasticity
blocks.cap: Try the buttons: any straight supply line through the origin has elasticity 1 everywhere; one that starts on the price axis is elastic; one that starts on the quantity axis is inelastic; and a vertical line has elasticity 0.

blocks.title: A midpoint calculation
blocks.q: When the price of strawberries rises from \$3 to \$5 a box, farms offer 140 boxes instead of 100. Find the price elasticity of supply.
steps: $E_s = \dfrac{33.3\%}{50\%} \approx 0.67$: inelastic.

blocks.title: Short run and long run
blocks.q: A sudden rise in the demand for electricians raises their pay. Why does the quantity of electrician hours supplied respond little this month but much more over five years?
steps: This month, the only extra hours come from overtime by people already trained.
Over five years, new people can train and get licensed, so many more hours become available.
Supply is more elastic with more time to adjust.
blocks.a: More time to train makes supply more elastic.

blocks.html: Giving supply elasticity a minus sign out of habit from demand, or thinking perfectly inelastic supply is horizontal. Price and quantity supplied move the same way, so $E_s$ is positive. "Inelastic" means quantity doesn't respond to price: whatever the price, the quantity is the same, which is a vertical line. Check: picture the price rising. If the quantity can't move, the curve must go straight up.

blocks.html: The same percent-change ratio (Price Elasticity of Demand) measures how demand responds to income and to the prices of related goods (Substitutes and Complements). This time the sign is the point.

Income elasticity $= \dfrac{\%\Delta Q_d}{\%\Delta \text{income}}$. Positive: a normal good (above 1, a luxury; between 0 and 1, a necessity). Negative: an inferior good. Cross-price elasticity of good X with respect to the price of Y $= \dfrac{\%\Delta Q_{d,X}}{\%\Delta P_Y}$. Positive: substitutes. Negative: complements. Near zero: unrelated. Keep the signs.

For price elasticity of demand the sign is always negative, so dropping it loses nothing. Here the sign is not known in advance; it carries the answer. If quantity rises when income rises, both changes are positive and so is the ratio: normal. If tea sales rise when coffee's price rises, both changes have the same sign: substitutes. Opposite directions give a negative ratio: inferior goods or complements.

blocks.name: ec-sort

cards.text: Income elasticity of restaurant meals: +1.5
cards.why: Positive income elasticity: a normal good (a luxury, since it is above 1).

cards.text: Income elasticity of long-distance bus trips: −0.4
cards.why: Negative: as incomes rise, people buy fewer.

cards.text: Income elasticity of bread: +0.2
cards.why: Positive but small: a normal good that is a necessity.

cards.text: Cross-price elasticity of tea with respect to the price of coffee: +0.6
cards.why: Pricier coffee, more tea: substitutes.

cards.text: Cross-price elasticity of coffee filters with respect to the price of coffee: −0.8
cards.why: Pricier coffee, fewer filters: complements.

cards.text: Cross-price elasticity of e-books with respect to the price of printed books: +0.9
cards.why: Positive: the two are substitutes.

blocks.cap: Sort each made-up elasticity by what its sign tells you.

blocks.title: Income elasticity
blocks.q: When average income in a town rises from \$40,000 to \$60,000, sales of a meal kit rise from 10,000 to 14,000 a month. Find the income elasticity (midpoint method) and classify the good.
steps: Income elasticity $\approx \dfrac{33.3\%}{40\%} \approx +0.83$: positive and below 1, a normal good and a necessity for these buyers.

blocks.title: Cross-price elasticity
blocks.q: The price of printers rises by 10%, and the quantity of ink cartridges demanded falls by 15%. Find the cross-price elasticity and say how the goods are related.
steps: $$\dfrac{\%\Delta Q_{\text{ink}}}{\%\Delta P_{\text{printers}}} = \dfrac{-15\%}{+10\%} = -1.5$$
Negative: complements, as you'd expect for goods used together.

blocks.html: Dropping the sign as you would for price elasticity of demand. An income elasticity of −0.4 and one of +0.4 describe opposite kinds of goods. Check: before dividing, write the sign of each percent change. Same signs give a positive ratio; opposite signs give a negative one.

blocks.html: At the market equilibrium (Market Equilibrium), most buyers would have paid more than the price, and most sellers would have sold for less. Those gaps are gains from trade, and on a graph they are areas, often triangles (Area of a Triangle).

Consumer surplus is the total of what buyers were willing to pay minus what they paid: the area below the demand curve and above the price, out to the quantity traded. Producer surplus is the total of the price minus the least each seller would accept: the area above the supply curve and below the price. With straight lines at equilibrium, each is a triangle: $\tfrac{1}{2} \times Q^* \times$ (the height between the price and the curve's intercept).

Line buyers up from the most eager to the least: the height of the demand curve at each quantity is what that buyer would pay for that unit. A buyer who would pay \$9 and pays \$6 gains \$3. Add those gains over every unit bought and you get the area between the demand curve and the price. The supply curve works the same way, because its height at each quantity is the lowest price that would get that unit sold, the seller's marginal cost.

blocks.name: ec-market
blocks.cap: Blue is consumer surplus, orange is producer surplus. Each is a triangle with base 8 (the quantity) and height \$4.

blocks.title: Counting buyer by buyer
blocks.q: Five buyers would pay at most \$10, \$8, \$7, \$5 and \$3 for one ticket each. The price is \$6. Find consumer surplus.
steps: Only buyers whose willingness to pay is at least \$6 buy: the \$10, \$8 and \$7 buyers.
Consumer surplus: $\$4 + \$2 + \$1 = \$7$.

blocks.title: Triangles from equations
blocks.q: $Q_d = 20 - 2P$ and $Q_s = -4 + 2P$, so the equilibrium is \$6 and 8 units. Find consumer and producer surplus.
steps: Demand meets the price axis at \$10 (set $Q_d = 0$); supply starts at \$2 (set $Q_s = 0$).

blocks.html: Confusing consumer surplus with spending. Buyers spend $\$6 \times 8 = \$48$; that's a rectangle under the price, and it is a transfer to sellers, not a gain. Consumer surplus is the triangle above the price. Also measure the triangle out to the quantity actually traded, not to where demand meets the axis. Check: surplus areas sit between a curve and the price line, and stop at the traded quantity.

blocks.html: Consumer and producer surplus (Consumer and Producer Surplus) add up to total surplus, the whole gain from trading in a market. A competitive market makes that total as large as it can be, as long as nobody outside the deal is affected.

Total surplus = consumer surplus + producer surplus = the area between demand and supply, out to the quantity traded. It is largest at the competitive equilibrium $Q^*$. If less (or more) than $Q^*$ is traded, some of it is lost. That lost surplus is the deadweight loss (DWL), a triangle between the curves: $$DWL = \tfrac{1}{2} \times (\text{gap between the curves at } Q) \times |Q^* - Q|.$$

For every unit up to $Q^*$, the demand curve (what a buyer would pay) is above the supply curve (what it costs a seller to provide). Trading that unit creates a gain equal to the gap. Stop at a smaller quantity and those gains never happen: no buyer gets them and no seller does. Past $Q^*$, each unit costs more to make than anyone would pay for it, so producing it destroys surplus. Either way the total shrinks by a triangle.

blocks.name: ec-market
blocks.cap: Only 5 units are traded instead of 8. The hatched triangle is the deadweight loss: gains from trade that nobody gets.

blocks.title: Too little traded
blocks.q: In the market $Q_d = 20 - 2P$, $Q_s = -4 + 2P$ (equilibrium 8 units), only 5 units are traded. Find the deadweight loss.
steps: Demand's height at 5: from $P = 10 - Q/2$, $P = 7.5$. Supply's height at 5: from $P = 2 + Q/2$, $P = 4.5$.
The gap is $\$7.50 - \$4.50 = \$3$, and the missing units run from 5 to 8.
$DWL = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 3 \times 3 = \$4.50$.

blocks.title: Too much traded
blocks.q: Same market, but 10 units are traded. Find the deadweight loss.
steps: At 10 units, demand's height is \$5 and supply's is \$7: those last 2 units cost more than buyers value them.

blocks.html: Thinking the lost surplus is money someone else collects. A deadweight loss is not a transfer; it's a gain that would have happened and didn't. When surplus moves from buyers to sellers (as with a higher price), it is redistributed, not lost. Check: ask "does anyone receive this area?" If no one does, it's deadweight loss.
"Efficient" here means the total gain is as large as possible. It says nothing about whether the split between buyers and sellers is fair; that's a normative question.

blocks.html: Governments sometimes set a legal price limit. Whether the limit changes anything depends on where it sits relative to equilibrium; when it does, it creates the shortages and surpluses of Shortages and Surpluses and the deadweight loss of Total Surplus and Deadweight Loss.

A price ceiling is a legal maximum price. It is binding only if it is below the equilibrium price; then quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied (a shortage), and only the quantity sellers offer is traded. A price floor is a legal minimum. It is binding only if it is above equilibrium; then there is a surplus, and only the quantity buyers want is traded. A binding control creates a deadweight loss.

A ceiling above the equilibrium price allows the market price, so it changes nothing. A ceiling below it forbids the equilibrium; at the legal price, sellers move down their supply curve and offer less, while buyers want more. The smaller side of the market decides how much changes hands, so trades that would benefit both sides don't happen. A floor works the same way from above.

blocks.name: ec-intervention
blocks.cap: A ceiling at \$4, below the \$6 equilibrium: a shortage of 8 and a deadweight loss. Drag the ceiling above \$6 and it stops binding.

blocks.title: A binding ceiling
blocks.q: $Q_d = 20 - 2P$ and $Q_s = -4 + 2P$ (equilibrium \$6, 8 units). The government sets a price ceiling of \$4. Find the shortage, the quantity traded and the deadweight loss.
steps: \$4 is below \$6, so the ceiling binds.
At \$4: $Q_d = 12$, $Q_s = 4$. Shortage: $12 - 4 = 8$. Only 4 are traded.
At 4 units, buyers would pay $10 - 4/2 = \$8$; sellers' cost is \$4.

blocks.title: A floor that does nothing
blocks.q: In the same market, a price floor of \$5 is set. What happens?
steps: A floor is a minimum. The market price, \$6, is already above \$5.
The floor doesn't bind: the market stays at \$6 and 8 units.

blocks.html: Placing a binding ceiling above the equilibrium because "ceiling" sounds high, or thinking a ceiling above equilibrium changes the market. A ceiling is a lid: it only matters if it pushes the price down. Check: a binding ceiling is below $P^*$ and a binding floor is above it.

Economists broadly agree that binding rent ceilings reduce the quantity and quality of rental housing over time. The minimum wage is a price floor in the labor market; in the competitive model it creates a surplus of labor, but the model in Monopsony predicts it can raise employment, and the measured effects of particular minimum wages are studied and debated.
