blocks.html: A per-unit tax (an excise tax) works like a supply shifter (What Shifts Supply): sellers now need more per unit to be willing to sell. The result is a smaller market, a gain for the government and a deadweight loss (Total Surplus and Deadweight Loss).

A tax of $t$ per unit drives a wedge between the price buyers pay, $P_b$, and the price sellers keep, $P_s$: $P_b - P_s = t$. The quantity falls to $Q_t$, where buyers' quantity at $P_b$ equals sellers' quantity at $P_s$. Tax revenue $= t \times Q_t$. Deadweight loss $= \tfrac{1}{2} \times t \times (Q^* - Q_t)$.

Collected from sellers, the tax means a seller who needed \$4 to sell a unit now needs \$4 plus the tax: the supply curve shifts up by $t$. The new crossing with demand gives the buyers' price and quantity; sellers keep that price minus $t$. Revenue is a rectangle of height $t$ and width $Q_t$, money that moves from buyers and sellers to the government. The units between $Q_t$ and $Q^*$ would have been worth more to buyers than they cost sellers, but the tax stops them: that triangle is lost.

blocks.name: ec-intervention
blocks.cap: A \$3 tax: buyers pay \$7.50, sellers keep \$4.50, 5 units are sold, revenue is \$15 and the deadweight loss is \$4.50. Slide the tax to see the triangle grow.

blocks.title: A \$3 tax
blocks.q: $Q_d = 20 - 2P$ and $Q_s = -4 + 2P$. A \$3 per-unit tax is collected from sellers. Find $P_b$, $P_s$, the quantity, the revenue and the deadweight loss.
steps: Sellers keep $P_b - 3$: set $20 - 2P_b = -4 + 2(P_b - 3)$.
Revenue $= \$3 \times 5 = \$15$. $DWL = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 3 \times (8 - 5) = \$4.50$.

blocks.title: Collected from buyers instead
blocks.q: Suppose the same \$3 tax is collected from buyers at the register. What changes?
steps: Now demand shifts down by \$3: buyers will pay sellers at most their old willingness minus the tax.
Solve $20 - 2(P_s + 3) = -4 + 2P_s$: $14 - 2P_s = -4 + 2P_s$, so $P_s = 4.5$ and buyers pay $4.5 + 3 = 7.5$ in total.
blocks.a: Nothing that matters: the same \$7.50, \$4.50 and 5 units.

blocks.html: Expecting the price to rise by the full tax, or computing revenue with the old quantity. Here the buyers' price rose by \$1.50, not \$3, and revenue is $3 \times 5$, not $3 \times 8 = \$24$. Check: $P_b - P_s$ must equal the tax, and both prices must give the same new quantity.

blocks.html: The excise tax in Per-Unit Taxes raised the buyers' price by part of the tax and lowered the sellers' price by the rest. How the burden splits depends on elasticity (Price Elasticity of Supply, Elastic, Inelastic and What Decides It), not on who writes the check.

Tax incidence is who really bears a tax. Buyers bear $P_b - P^*$ per unit and sellers bear $P^* - P_s$; the two add up to the tax. The less elastic side of the market bears more of the tax, whoever is legally required to pay it.

A tax pushes buyers and sellers apart. Whichever side can more easily walk away (buy a substitute, or sell something else) does, and so avoids most of the tax; the side with few alternatives is stuck absorbing it. If demand is very inelastic, like demand for gasoline in the short run, buyers keep buying, and the price they pay rises by nearly the whole tax. If supply is very inelastic, like the supply of land, sellers can't reduce what they offer, and their price falls by nearly the whole tax.

blocks.name: ec-intervention
blocks.cap: Here supply is more elastic than demand at the equilibrium. Of the \$3 tax, buyers bear \$2 and sellers \$1. Switch who sends the check: the split doesn't change.

blocks.title: Splitting a \$3 tax
blocks.q: $Q_d = 24 - P$ and $Q_s = -6 + 2P$. A \$3 tax is collected from sellers. How much of it do buyers bear?
steps: Before the tax: $24 - P = -6 + 2P$, so $P^* = 10$ and $Q^* = 14$.
Buyers bear $\$12 - \$10 = \$2$ per unit ($\tfrac{2}{3}$); sellers bear $\$10 - \$9 = \$1$ ($\tfrac{1}{3}$).
At $P^* = 10$, $Q^* = 14$: demand's elasticity is $1 \times \tfrac{10}{14} \approx 0.71$ and supply's is $2 \times \tfrac{10}{14} \approx 1.43$. Buyers, the less elastic side, bear more.

blocks.title: Reasoning without numbers
blocks.q: A city taxes each pack of cigarettes, collected from stores. Smokers' demand is very inelastic, while stores can easily sell other products. Who bears most of the tax?
steps: Demand is the less elastic side.
So the price smokers pay rises by most of the tax, and stores' price falls only a little.
blocks.a: Mostly the smokers, although the stores send in the money.

blocks.html: Thinking whoever is legally required to pay the tax also bears its burden. The law decides who sends the check; the elasticities decide who ends up poorer. A payroll tax split "half and half" on paper falls mostly on workers if labor supply is less elastic than labor demand. Check: compare the price each side ends up with to the old equilibrium price.

blocks.html: A per-unit subsidy is a tax in reverse (Per-Unit Taxes): the government pays for each unit, so the market grows. Buyers and sellers both gain, but there is a bill.

A subsidy of $s$ per unit makes the price sellers receive exceed the price buyers pay: $P_s - P_b = s$. Quantity rises above $Q^*$. The cost to taxpayers is $s \times Q_s$. Buyers' and sellers' gains together are less than that cost; the difference is the deadweight loss, $\tfrac{1}{2} \times s \times (Q_s - Q^*)$.

Paid to sellers, the subsidy lowers the price each one needs by $s$: supply shifts down. Buyers pay less, sellers receive more, and more is traded. But the extra units between $Q^*$ and $Q_s$ cost more to produce than buyers value them, which is why the market didn't produce them before. The government pays for the whole rectangle $s \times Q_s$, while buyers and sellers gain only part of it; the leftover triangle is the deadweight loss.

blocks.name: ec-intervention
blocks.cap: A \$2 subsidy: buyers pay \$5, sellers receive \$7, and 10 units are traded. The government's cost (red) reaches past the demand curve; the hatched triangle is the deadweight loss.

blocks.title: A \$2 subsidy
blocks.q: $Q_d = 20 - 2P$ and $Q_s = -4 + 2P$. The government pays sellers \$2 per unit. Find $P_b$, $P_s$, the quantity, the cost to taxpayers and the deadweight loss.
steps: Sellers receive $P_b + 2$: $20 - 2P_b = -4 + 2(P_b + 2)$, so $20 = 4P_b$ and $P_b = 5$; $P_s = 7$.
Cost to taxpayers: $\$2 \times 10 = \$20$.
$DWL = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 2 \times (10 - 8) = \$2$.

blocks.title: Where did the \$20 go?
blocks.q: In the same market, how much do consumer and producer surplus rise?
steps: Before: $CS = PS = \$16$ (from Consumer and Producer Surplus).
After: $CS = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 10 \times (\$10 - \$5) = \$25$ and $PS = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 10 \times (\$7 - \$2) = \$25$.
Gains: \$9 each, \$18 in all, against a \$20 cost. The missing \$2 is the deadweight loss.
blocks.a: Each rises by \$9; together \$18, less than the \$20 cost.

blocks.html: Counting the gains to buyers and sellers but forgetting the cost to taxpayers, and so concluding that a subsidy must raise total surplus. In a market with no spillovers it lowers total surplus. Check: always subtract the government's cost, $s \times Q_s$.
When a good benefits people outside the market, such as vaccines, the case changes: a subsidy can move the market toward the efficient amount. That is the subject of Positive Externalities.

blocks.html: Trade between countries creates gains overall (Specialization and the Terms of Trade). One market's supply and demand graph, with the surplus areas from Total Surplus and Deadweight Loss, shows who gains and who loses when a country opens to trade.

A small country that opens to trade takes the world price $P_w$ as given. If $P_w$ is below its own equilibrium price, the country imports $Q_d - Q_s$ at $P_w$: consumers gain, domestic producers lose, and consumers gain more than producers lose. If $P_w$ is above, it exports $Q_s - Q_d$: producers gain more than consumers lose.

With imports, the price falls to $P_w$. Buyers pay less on every unit and buy more, so consumer surplus grows a lot. Domestic sellers get less and sell less, so producer surplus shrinks. The rectangle between the old and new price on domestic sales just moves from producers to consumers. Consumers also gain a triangle on the extra imported units, and nobody loses that one: it's the net gain from trade.

blocks.name: ec-intervention
blocks.cap: At a world price of \$4, the country buys 12 units, makes 4 and imports 8. Drag the world price above \$6 to see exports instead.

blocks.title: Opening to imports
blocks.q: $Q_d = 20 - 2P$, $Q_s = -4 + 2P$ (equilibrium \$6, 8 units). The country opens to trade at a world price of \$4. Find imports and the changes in consumer and producer surplus.
steps: At \$4: $Q_d = 12$, $Q_s = 4$, so imports are $12 - 4 = 8$.
Consumer surplus: from $\tfrac{1}{2}(8)(4) = \$16$ to $\tfrac{1}{2}(12)(10 - 4) = \$36$, a gain of \$20.
Producer surplus: from \$16 to $\tfrac{1}{2}(4)(4 - 2) = \$4$, a loss of \$12.
Net gain: $\$20 - \$12 = \$8$, the triangle $\tfrac{1}{2} \times (6 - 4) \times (12 - 4)$.

blocks.title: Opening to exports
blocks.q: Same market, but the world price is \$8. What happens?
steps: At \$8: $Q_d = 4$ and $Q_s = 12$. The country exports $12 - 4 = 8$.
Domestic buyers now pay \$8 and buy less; producers sell more at a higher price.
blocks.a: Exports of 8; producers gain, domestic consumers lose, and the gain is larger.

blocks.html: Seeing only the loss to domestic producers and concluding the country as a whole is worse off. In the model, consumers' gain is bigger than producers' loss. But the losses are real and concentrated: particular workers and firms bear them, sometimes for years, while the gains are spread across many buyers. Check: compute both changes and add them.
Economists broadly agree on the net gain in this model. How large and lasting the losses are for workers in import-competing industries, and how best to help them, are actively studied and debated.

blocks.html: A country that imports at the world price (Trade at the World Price) can restrict trade with a tax on imports, a tariff, or a limit on their quantity, a quota. Both work like the excise tax of Per-Unit Taxes, applied only to imports.

A tariff of $t$ per unit raises the domestic price to $P_w + t$. Domestic producers sell more, consumers buy less, imports fall. The government collects $t \times$ (new imports). Total surplus falls by two deadweight-loss triangles: one from inefficient domestic production, one from consumption given up. A quota that allows the same imports raises the price the same way, but the rectangle goes to whoever holds the import licenses (the quota rent), not the government.

With the tariff, a foreign seller needs $P_w + t$ to cover the tax, so that becomes the domestic price. At the higher price, domestic firms expand, even though some of their extra units cost more to make than the world price: that's the production triangle. Buyers cut back on units they valued above the world price: the consumption triangle. A quota creates scarcity of imports directly; the price rises until the quantity demanded minus domestic supply equals the quota.

blocks.name: ec-intervention
blocks.cap: A \$1 tariff on a \$3 world price. The price rises to \$4, imports fall from 12 to 8, the government collects \$8 (gold) and two small triangles are lost.

blocks.title: A \$1 tariff
blocks.q: $Q_d = 20 - 2P$, $Q_s = -4 + 2P$, world price \$3. A \$1 tariff is imposed. Find imports before and after, the tariff revenue and the deadweight loss.
steps: Before: at \$3, $Q_d = 14$, $Q_s = 2$, imports 12.
After: the price is \$4. $Q_d = 12$, $Q_s = 4$, imports 8.
Revenue: $\$1 \times 8 = \$8$.

blocks.title: The matching quota
blocks.q: Instead of the tariff, the country allows only 8 units of imports. What is the domestic price, and who gets the \$8 rectangle?
steps: Imports equal $Q_d - Q_s = (20 - 2P) - (-4 + 2P) = 24 - 4P$.
Set $24 - 4P = 8$: $P = \$4$, the same as with the tariff.
The gap between \$4 and the \$3 world price on 8 imported units, \$8, goes to license holders.
blocks.a: \$4; the \$8 goes to whoever holds the import licenses.

blocks.html: Thinking foreign producers pay the tariff. The importer sends the tax to the government, and in this model the domestic price rises by the full tariff, so domestic buyers bear it. Also, missing that a quota raises the price just like a tariff but hands the rectangle to license holders instead of the government. Check: who pays the higher domestic price? Buyers at home.

Economists broadly agree that tariffs raise domestic prices and create deadweight losses. Arguments for some protection (national security, young industries, a response to other countries' barriers) are debated, and the answers depend on the case.

blocks.html: A business's costs include more than the bills it pays. Opportunity cost (Opportunity Cost) says the owner's own time and money have a cost too: whatever they could have earned elsewhere.

Explicit costs are payments to others: wages, rent, materials. Implicit costs are the opportunity costs of resources the owners supply themselves, such as the salary the owner gave up or the interest their savings could have earned. $$\text{Accounting profit} = TR - \text{explicit costs}$$ $$\text{Economic profit} = TR - (\text{explicit costs}) - (\text{implicit costs})$$ Zero economic profit is a normal profit: the owners earn exactly what their resources would earn in their best other use.

An owner who quits a \$60,000 job to run a shop has given up \$60,000 a year, even though no one sends her a bill for it. If the shop's accounting profit is \$50,000, she is \$10,000 a year worse off than if she had kept her job. Economic profit counts that, so it answers the real question, "is this the best use of what I have?" Zero economic profit means "as good as the next best option," which is why firms can be content with it.

blocks.title: Accounting versus economic profit
blocks.q: Rosa's café earns \$200,000 in revenue. She pays \$150,000 for staff, rent and supplies. To run it, she gave up a \$60,000 salary. Find accounting and economic profit.
steps: Implicit cost: the \$60,000 salary.

blocks.title: Money and time
blocks.q: Jin earns \$90,000 in revenue from a repair shop with \$40,000 of explicit costs. He gave up a \$35,000 job and put \$50,000 of savings into equipment instead of an account paying 4% a year. Find his economic profit.
blocks.a: \$13,000: the shop beats his next best option.

blocks.html: Leaving out implicit costs, and thinking zero economic profit means the business is failing. A firm with zero economic profit covers every cost, including a normal return on the owner's time and money. Check: list every resource the owner provides, and ask what it would earn elsewhere.

blocks.html: Before costs, there is production: how much output a firm gets from its inputs. The marginal idea from Marginal Benefit, Marginal Cost and Sunk Costs applies here too, one worker at a time.

In the short run at least one input, such as the size of the plant, is fixed. Total product (TP) is the output. Marginal product of labor is the extra output from one more worker, $MP = \Delta TP / \Delta L$. Average product is $AP = TP / L$. The law of diminishing marginal returns: as more workers are added to a fixed plant, eventually each adds less than the one before.

With one oven and one cook, a second cook helps a lot: one rolls dough while the other bakes. A third still helps. But the oven doesn't grow. By the sixth cook, people are waiting for oven space, so each new cook adds less. Pile in enough and they get in each other's way; marginal product can even turn negative. The cause is the fixed input: each new worker has less of it to work with.

steps: $MP$ of worker 3: $36 - 24 = 12$ units.
$AP$ of 4 workers: $44 \div 4 = 11$ units per worker.
MP goes 10, 14, 12, 8, …: it is highest for worker 2 and falls from worker 3 on. Diminishing marginal returns begin with the third worker.

blocks.title: Diminishing is not negative

steps: Worker 5 adds 4 units, worker 6 adds 0, worker 7 adds −4.
Diminishing returns started long before worker 5, yet worker 5 still adds output. Only worker 7 lowers it.
Whether hiring pays depends on wages and prices too, which comes later (Marginal Revenue Product and Hiring).
blocks.a: Worker 5 adds output; worker 6 adds nothing; worker 7 reduces it.

blocks.html: Confusing diminishing marginal returns (marginal product falling) with negative returns (total product falling), or with diseconomies of scale, a long-run idea about the size of the whole firm. Check: diminishing returns means the MP numbers shrink while staying positive; total product still rises.

blocks.html: Production (Short-Run Production) turns into costs once you pay for inputs. The costs a firm counts include implicit ones (Accounting and Economic Profit).

Fixed cost (FC) doesn't change with output in the short run; variable cost (VC) does; $TC = FC + VC$. Per unit: $AFC = FC/q$, $AVC = VC/q$, $ATC = TC/q = AFC + AVC$. Marginal cost is the extra cost of one more unit: $MC = \Delta TC / \Delta q$, which equals $\Delta VC / \Delta q$ because fixed cost doesn't change.

Marginal cost mirrors marginal product. If a worker costs \$20 an hour and the next worker adds 4 units an hour, those units cost \$5 each. When marginal product rises, marginal cost falls; once diminishing returns set in, marginal cost rises. That's why MC curves are U-shaped. Fixed cost has no "marginal" part: you pay it whether you make 0 units or 100.

blocks.html: The cost curves from Short-Run Costs fit together in a pattern. Once you see why, you can sketch them from memory.

When marginal cost is below an average, the average falls; when it is above, the average rises. So MC crosses AVC and ATC at their lowest points. AFC falls the whole way, so the gap between ATC and AVC (which equals AFC) narrows as output grows.

Think of a running grade average. If your average is 80 and you score 70 on the next test, your average falls; score 90, and it rises. The next test is the "marginal" score. Costs work the same way: each new unit's cost (MC) pulls the average cost toward it. The average stops falling and starts rising exactly when MC moves from below it to above it, which is the bottom of the average curve.

blocks.cap: MC (orange) crosses AVC and ATC at their lowest points. Move the marker: wherever MC is below ATC, ATC slopes down.

blocks.title: Grades as a model
blocks.q: A student's average over four tests is 80. The fifth test scores 70. What happens to the average? What if it scores 95?
steps: Total so far: $4 \times 80 = 320$.
A marginal value below the average pulls it down; above it pulls it up.

blocks.title: Find the bottom of ATC
blocks.q: In the table from the last lesson, ATC is \$50, \$31, \$24, \$21, \$22, \$24 for 1 to 6 units, and MC is \$20, \$12, \$10, \$12, \$26, \$34. Where is ATC lowest, and how does MC explain it?
steps: ATC is lowest at 4 units (\$21).
The 4th unit's MC (\$12) is below the average before it (\$24), so ATC falls to \$21.
The 5th unit's MC (\$26) is above \$21, so ATC rises to \$22. MC crosses ATC between 4 and 5 units, at the bottom.
blocks.a: At 4 units; MC passes from below ATC to above it there.

blocks.html: Thinking marginal cost is at its lowest where it crosses average total cost. The crossing is at the lowest point of the average; MC's own minimum comes earlier, at a smaller quantity. Check on the picture: MC is already rising where it meets ATC.

blocks.html: Knowing how the curves fit together (How Marginal and Average Costs Relate) lets you predict what a cost change does. The key is whether the change depends on how much the firm makes.

A change in fixed cost (rent, a license fee, a lump-sum tax) shifts AFC and ATC only. MC and AVC don't move, so the quantity that maximizes profit doesn't change. A change in variable cost (wages, materials, a per-unit tax) shifts MC, AVC and ATC.

Marginal cost is the change in total cost from one more unit. A \$500 license fee is paid whether the firm makes 10 units or 100, so it adds nothing to the cost of the next unit: MC is unchanged, and so is AVC, which only counts variable cost. Spread over the units, though, the fee raises the average total cost, by \$500 ÷ q. A \$2 per-unit tax, by contrast, adds \$2 to the cost of every unit, so MC, AVC and ATC all rise by \$2.

blocks.title: A license fee
blocks.q: A food truck's city license rises from \$600 to \$1,000 a year. It sells 2,000 meals a year. What happens to its MC, AVC and ATC at 2,000 meals?
steps: The fee is a fixed cost: MC and AVC don't change.
ATC rises by $\$400 \div 2{,}000 = \$0.20$ per meal.
Since MC didn't move, the best quantity doesn't change in the short run.
blocks.a: MC and AVC unchanged; ATC up \$0.20.

blocks.title: A per-unit tax
blocks.q: A city adds a \$0.50 tax on each meal sold. What happens to MC, AVC and ATC?
steps: Every meal now costs \$0.50 more to sell, so the tax is a variable cost.
MC, AVC and ATC each rise by \$0.50 at every quantity.

blocks.html: Shifting MC when fixed cost changes, and so predicting that a lump-sum fee changes how much a firm produces. Check: ask "does this cost change with the number of units?" If not, it can't change the cost of one more unit.
In the long run a big enough fixed cost can matter: if price no longer covers ATC, some firms leave the industry (Entry, Exit and the Long Run).

blocks.html: In the long run a firm can change everything, including the size of its plant. The question shifts from "how much from this factory?" (How Marginal and Average Costs Relate) to "how big should the firm be?"

The long-run average total cost (LRATC) curve shows the lowest average cost of each output when all inputs can vary. Where LRATC falls as output grows, there are economies of scale; where it is flat, constant returns to scale; where it rises, diseconomies of scale. The minimum efficient scale is the smallest output at which LRATC reaches its lowest level.

Bigger firms can split work into specialized jobs, use large machines that only pay off at high volume, and buy inputs in bulk: average cost falls. Past some size, a firm gets hard to manage: more layers of bosses, slower decisions, workers far from the customers, so average cost can rise. The long-run curve is made from short-run curves: for each output, the firm picks the plant size with the lowest ATC, so LRATC is the lower edge of all the short-run ATC curves.

That is the seed of a natural monopoly (Regulating a Natural Monopoly).

blocks.html: Confusing diseconomies of scale with diminishing marginal returns. Diminishing returns is a short-run idea: adding workers to a fixed plant. Diseconomies of scale is a long-run idea: growing the whole firm, plant and all, and finding average cost rising. Check: ask whether any input is held fixed. If yes, it's diminishing returns.

blocks.html: Market supply and demand set a price (Market Equilibrium). Now zoom in on one seller among thousands. With so many sellers of the same thing, any one seller's buyers have perfect substitutes, the most elastic case of Elastic, Inelastic and What Decides It.

Perfect competition: many small firms, an identical product, easy entry and exit, and buyers and sellers who know the prices. Each firm is a price taker: it can sell as much as it wants at the market price and nothing above it. Its own demand curve is horizontal at the market price, so for the firm $P = MR = AR$.

A wheat farm grows a tiny share of the world's wheat. If it asks a penny above the market price, buyers simply buy identical wheat from someone else, so it sells nothing. If it charges less, it gives money away, because it can already sell all it grows at the market price. So every extra bushel brings in exactly the market price: marginal revenue equals price. The market's demand curve still slopes down; it's the single firm's slice of it that looks flat.

blocks.name: ec-firmmarket
blocks.cap: Left: the market, where supply and demand set the price. Right: one firm, which takes that price as a flat line, $P = MR = d$.

blocks.title: Revenue for a price taker
blocks.q: Wheat sells for \$6 a bushel. A farm sells 2,000 bushels. Find its total revenue, average revenue and the marginal revenue of one more bushel.
steps: $AR = TR \div Q = \$6$.
One more bushel sells for \$6, without lowering the price on the others: $MR = \$6$.

blocks.title: Which markets come close?
blocks.q: Which comes closer to perfect competition: farms selling a grade of corn, or the market for smartphones?
steps: Corn of one grade is identical whoever grows it; there are many farms, and none can affect the price.
Smartphones differ by brand and features, and a few large firms set their own prices.
blocks.a: Corn. No real market is perfectly competitive, but some come close.

blocks.html: Giving the single firm a downward-sloping demand curve because the market demand curve slopes down. The market's curve does slope down, but one small firm's output is too little to move the market price, so the firm faces a flat line. Check: ask "if this firm doubled its output, would the market price change?" For a price taker, no.

blocks.html: A price taker (Perfect Competition and Price Takers) can't choose its price, only its quantity. The marginal rule from Marginal Benefit, Marginal Cost and Sunk Costs, with the cost curves from How Marginal and Average Costs Relate, tells it how much to make.
To maximize profit, produce every unit whose marginal revenue is at least its marginal cost, and stop where $MR = MC$ (on the rising part of MC). For a price taker $MR = P$, so the rule is $P = MC$.

Each unit changes profit by $MR - MC$. If a unit brings in more than it costs, making it adds to profit; if it costs more than it brings in, it subtracts. So profit grows until the last unit where $MR \ge MC$ and shrinks after. That point is not where revenue is largest (revenue keeps rising as long as you sell more) and not where profit per unit is largest (that's at the bottom of ATC).

blocks.title: Not the most revenue, not the most per unit
blocks.q: At 6 units revenue is highest (\$168). At 4 units, profit per unit ($P - ATC = \$28 - \$21$) is highest. Why choose 5?
steps: At 6 units, revenue rises \$28 but cost rises \$34: profit falls by \$6.
At 4 units, the 5th unit would add \$28 of revenue for \$26 of cost: \$2 of profit left on the table.
blocks.a: Total profit, not revenue or profit per unit, is the goal; MR = MC finds it.

blocks.html: Picking the output with the highest total revenue or the highest profit per unit instead of the one where $MR = MC$. Check: for the quantity you picked, the next unit's MC should be above the price, and the last unit's MC at or below it.

blocks.html: Once the firm has its quantity from $P = MC$ (Profit-Maximizing Output: MR = MC), the cost curves show its profit as an area. Remember that these are economic profits (Accounting and Economic Profit).

$$\text{Profit} = TR - TC = (P - ATC) \times q.$$ On the graph, profit is a rectangle: height $P - ATC$ at the chosen quantity, width $q$. If $P > ATC$ the firm earns a profit; if $P < ATC$, a loss; if $P = ATC$, zero economic profit (it breaks even). The break-even price is the minimum of ATC.

Total revenue is $P \times q$ and total cost is $ATC \times q$, because ATC is cost per unit. Subtract, and $q$ factors out: profit per unit times the number of units. The height uses ATC, not MC, because profit counts the cost of every unit, while MC is the cost of only the last one.

blocks.name: ec-costcurves
blocks.cap: The shaded rectangle is profit: price minus ATC, times quantity. Lower the price below the bottom of ATC and the rectangle becomes a loss.

blocks.title: A profit
blocks.q: A firm sells 8 units at \$30 each. At 8 units its ATC is \$24. Find its profit.
steps: Profit per unit: $\$30 - \$24 = \$6$.
Profit: $\$6 \times 8 = \$48$. Check: $TR = \$240$, $TC = \$24 \times 8 = \$192$, difference \$48.

blocks.title: A loss
blocks.q: The price falls to \$20. The firm now makes 6 units, where ATC is \$23. Find its profit.
steps: Profit: $-\$3 \times 6 = -\$18$, a loss of \$18.

blocks.html: A loss doesn't automatically mean the firm should close. Whether it keeps producing in the short run depends on which costs it would still have to pay if it shut down, which is the subject of The Shutdown Rule.

Measuring profit per unit as price minus marginal cost. At the chosen quantity $P = MC$, so that would always give zero. Profit per unit is $P - ATC$. Check: profit must equal $TR - TC$; compute both to confirm.

sources.name: OpenStax Principles of Microeconomics 3e, 8.2 How Perfectly Competitive Firms Make Output Decisions

blocks.html: A firm making a loss (Profit and Loss on the Graph) has a choice: keep producing, or shut down for now. The answer depends on which costs it would still have to pay.

In the short run, a firm shut down still pays its fixed costs, so its loss is $FC$. It should keep producing as long as the price covers average variable cost ($P \ge \min AVC$), even at a loss. It should shut down if $P < \min AVC$. The shutdown price is the minimum of AVC; the break-even price is the minimum of ATC.

Rent and loan payments are due whether the doors are open or not. Producing is worth it if the revenue at least covers the extra costs of producing, the variable costs, because anything left over helps pay the fixed costs. If price is below AVC, every unit made loses money on top of the fixed costs, so closing loses less. That's why a competitive firm's short-run supply curve is its MC curve above the minimum of AVC.

blocks.name: ec-costcurves
blocks.cap: At this price the firm loses money but covers AVC, so it keeps producing. Slide the price below the bottom of AVC: shutting down becomes the better choice. The thick part of MC is the firm's supply curve.

blocks.title: Keep going at a loss
blocks.q: A firm's fixed cost is \$100. At its best output it would earn \$300 in revenue and pay \$260 in variable costs. Should it produce?
steps: If it shuts down: profit $= -\$100$ (it still pays the fixed cost).
A \$60 loss beats a \$100 loss. Revenue covers variable cost, with \$40 toward fixed cost.

blocks.title: Time to close
blocks.q: A firm's AVC is at least \$12 at every output, and the price falls to \$10. What should it do in the short run?
steps: At \$10, every unit sells for less than its average variable cost.
Producing adds to the loss on top of fixed costs, so the firm should shut down and lose only its fixed cost.
blocks.a: Shut down until the price recovers.

blocks.html: Thinking a firm should shut down as soon as it makes a loss. In the short run it pays its fixed costs either way. Check: compare the loss from producing with the fixed cost. Produce whenever the loss is smaller, which is when $P \ge AVC$.
In the long run there are no fixed costs: leases end, equipment can be sold. A firm that expects losses to continue leaves the industry, which is the subject of the next lesson.

sources.name: OpenStax Principles of Microeconomics 3e, 8.2 How Perfectly Competitive Firms Make Output Decisions

blocks.html: The short run takes the number of firms as fixed (The Shutdown Rule). In the long run firms can enter and exit, and every firm can choose its scale (Economies and Diseconomies of Scale). That changes where price ends up.

If firms earn economic profits, new firms enter; market supply shifts right and the price falls. If they make losses, firms exit; supply shifts left and the price rises. Entry and exit stop when the price equals minimum ATC: in long-run equilibrium, each firm earns zero economic profit and produces at the bottom of its ATC curve.

Economic profit means the industry pays better than the best alternative use of the owners' time and money, so outsiders want in. Each new firm adds to market supply, pushing the price down, until the extra return is gone. Losses work in reverse. Zero economic profit is not zero reward: every owner still earns a normal return, as much as they could get anywhere else.

blocks.name: ec-firmmarket
blocks.cap: Step through it: demand rises, the price rises, firms earn profits, new firms enter, market supply shifts right, and the price falls back to minimum ATC. The firm's cost curves never move.

blocks.title: The long-run price and the number of firms
blocks.q: Each firm's ATC is lowest at 10 units, where it is \$20. Market demand is $Q_d = 1{,}000 - 25P$. In long-run equilibrium, what is the price, and how many firms are there?
steps: Long run: $P = \min ATC = \$20$.
Market quantity: $Q_d = 1{,}000 - 25(20) = 500$.
Each firm makes 10 units, so there are $500 \div 10 = 50$ firms.

blocks.title: After a demand increase
blocks.q: From that equilibrium, demand increases. What happens in the short run and the long run?
steps: Short run: the price rises above \$20; each firm moves up its MC curve and earns a profit.
Long run: profits attract entry; market supply shifts right until the price is back at \$20.
More firms, each making 10 units again; the market quantity is larger.
blocks.a: The price rises, then returns to \$20 with more firms.

blocks.html: Two mix-ups. Treating zero economic profit as no reward for owners; it includes a normal return on their resources. And shifting the firm's cost curves when firms enter; entry adds firms, which shifts the market supply curve. Each firm's costs stay the same. Check: in the long-run story, the only curves that move are on the market graph.

blocks.html: Long-run competitive equilibrium (Entry, Exit and the Long Run) has two special features. Each matches a kind of efficiency, and the first is the same total-surplus idea as in Total Surplus and Deadweight Loss.

Allocative efficiency: $P = MC$. The value buyers put on the last unit (the price) equals the cost of making it, so the right amount is produced and total surplus is as large as it can be. Productive efficiency: production at minimum ATC, the lowest possible cost per unit. In long-run equilibrium, perfect competition achieves both.

If $P > MC$, someone values one more unit more than it costs to make, so producing it would add surplus: too little is being made. If $P < MC$, the last unit cost more than it is worth: too much. Only at $P = MC$ is there no gain left. Productive efficiency is about cost: at the bottom of ATC, the goods are made with the fewest resources per unit. Competitive firms set $P = MC$ to maximize profit, and entry pushes $P$ down to minimum ATC, so both happen without anyone planning them.

blocks.name: ec-firmmarket
blocks.cap: At the end of the long-run story, the firm sits where $P = MC$ (allocative efficiency) and $P = \min ATC$ (productive efficiency).

blocks.title: Check both conditions
blocks.q: A firm sells at \$15. At its output, MC is \$15 and ATC is \$18, while its minimum ATC is \$14. Is it allocatively efficient? Productively efficient?
steps: $P = MC = \$15$: allocatively efficient.
ATC at its output (\$18) is above the minimum (\$14): not productively efficient.
It also has a loss of \$3 per unit, so in the long run firms will exit.
blocks.a: Allocatively efficient, but not productively efficient.

blocks.title: Efficiency is not fairness
blocks.q: A market reaches the competitive outcome. Does that make the outcome fair?
steps: Efficiency is about the size of the total gain.
Fairness is about how gains are shared; a market can be efficient while some people end up with very little.
Whether and how to redistribute is a normative question.
blocks.a: Not necessarily: efficient and fair are different questions.

blocks.html: Mixing up the two conditions, or thinking an efficient outcome must also be fair. Allocative means $P = MC$ (the right amount); productive means minimum ATC (the cheapest way). Check: name the comparison. Price against marginal cost, or average cost against its minimum.

sources.name: OpenStax Principles of Microeconomics 3e, 8.4 Efficiency in Perfectly Competitive Markets

blocks.html: In perfect competition, profits invite entry until they disappear (Entry, Exit and the Long Run). A monopoly is the opposite extreme: a single seller of a good with no close substitutes, protected by something that keeps rivals out.

A monopoly lasts only behind barriers to entry: economies of scale so large that one firm can serve the market most cheaply (a natural monopoly), legal protection such as patents, copyrights and exclusive licenses, control of a key resource, and network effects, where a product is more valuable the more people use it. A monopoly still faces the downward-sloping market demand curve.

Without a barrier, a monopoly's profits would draw in rivals, just as they do in a competitive industry. Patents are a deliberate trade: inventors get a temporary monopoly (20 years from filing in the United States) as a reward for creating something new. Network effects work because buyers want what everyone else uses: a messaging app with all your friends on it beats a better app with none.

cards.text: A drug company holds a patent on a new medicine
cards.why: A patent legally bars others from making the drug for a period of years.

cards.text: One water system’s pipes serve a whole town
cards.why: A second set of pipes would double the cost; one firm serves everyone most cheaply.

cards.text: A company owns the only mine of a rare mineral
cards.why: Rivals can’t get the input.

cards.text: Everyone joins the social app their friends already use
cards.why: The product is worth more because so many others use it.

cards.text: An author’s copyright on a best-selling novel
cards.why: Copyright gives exclusive rights to copy the work.

cards.text: A power company spreads huge plant costs over a whole region
cards.why: Average cost keeps falling as one firm serves more customers.

blocks.cap: Sort each monopoly by the barrier that protects it.

blocks.title: Name the barrier
blocks.q: What keeps rivals out in each case? (a) A city grants one company the only taxi license at the airport. (b) A rail line between two cities, where building a second track would cost billions. (c) A video-game console that has the most games because it has the most players.
steps: (a) Legal protection: an exclusive license.
(b) Economies of scale: one line can carry all the traffic at the lowest cost per trip.
(c) Network effects: game makers go where the players are, and players go where the games are.
blocks.a: (a) legal, (b) economies of scale, (c) network effects.

blocks.html: Thinking a monopoly can charge any price it likes. It is the only seller, but buyers still decide how much to buy at each price: it faces the whole market demand curve. Raise the price and it sells less. Check: a monopolist picks a point on the demand curve; it can't pick a price and a quantity separately.
Governments also limit monopoly power through antitrust law, which can block mergers and forbid tactics such as agreeing with rivals to fix prices. How strictly to enforce it is debated.

blocks.html: For a price taker, one more unit brings in the price. A monopoly faces the whole downward-sloping demand curve (Monopoly and Barriers to Entry), so to sell one more unit it must lower the price, the same tradeoff behind Elasticity and Total Revenue.

For a single-price seller, marginal revenue is less than price (after the first unit): selling one more unit means cutting the price on every unit. With linear demand $P = a - bQ$, marginal revenue is $$MR = a - 2bQ,$$ the same intercept and twice the slope. MR is zero at the middle of the demand line, where demand is unit elastic, and negative below it.

Suppose a seller can sell 4 units at \$8 or 5 units at \$7. The 5th unit brings in \$7 (the gain), but the first 4 units now sell for \$1 less each, losing \$4. So $MR = \$7 - \$4 = \$3$, well below the \$7 price. For linear demand, total revenue is $TR = aQ - bQ^2$, and its rate of change is $a - 2bQ$. Where demand is inelastic, cutting the price lowers revenue, so MR is negative there.

blocks.name: ec-monopoly
blocks.cap: Selling a 5th unit: the gain rectangle (the new unit at the lower price) minus the loss rectangle (the price cut on the first 4 units) is the marginal revenue.

blocks.title: From a demand schedule
blocks.q: Using the table, find the marginal revenue of the 4th unit and explain why it is less than \$7.
steps: The 4th unit sells for \$7 (gain), but the first 3 units drop from \$8 to \$7, losing $3 \times \$1 = \$3$.

blocks.title: From a linear demand curve
blocks.q: Demand is $P = 20 - 2Q$. Find marginal revenue at $Q = 3$, and the quantity where MR is zero.
steps: $MR = 0$ when $4Q = 20$, so $Q = 5$, the middle of the demand line (it reaches the quantity axis at 10).

blocks.html: Setting marginal revenue equal to price, as for a price taker. That forgets the revenue lost on the units that could have sold at the higher price. Check: for linear demand, MR must hit the quantity axis halfway to where demand does.

blocks.html: A monopoly maximizes profit with the same marginal rule as any firm, using its own marginal revenue (Why Marginal Revenue Is Below Price) and measuring profit as in Profit and Loss on the Graph.
(1) Find the quantity where $MR = MC$. (2) Go up to the demand curve at that quantity to read the price. (3) Profit $= (P - ATC) \times Q$.

Each unit adds $MR - MC$ to profit, so the monopoly keeps going while MR is at least MC, just like a competitive firm. The difference is the price: MR and MC tell the monopoly how many to sell, but the price it can charge for that many is whatever buyers will pay, and that is the height of the demand curve. Because MR is below demand, the price ends up above MC.

blocks.name: ec-monopoly
blocks.cap: MR meets MC at 8 units; the dotted line goes up to demand for the price, \$12. The gold rectangle is profit.

blocks.title: Constant marginal cost
blocks.q: A monopoly faces demand $P = 20 - Q$ and has a constant marginal cost of \$4, with no fixed cost. Find its quantity, price and profit.
steps: Price from demand: $P = 20 - 8 = \$12$.
With constant MC and no fixed cost, $ATC = \$4$. Profit $= (\$12 - \$4) \times 8 = \$64$.

blocks.title: With a fixed cost
blocks.q: Same monopoly, but it also has a fixed cost of \$40. Do its quantity and price change? What is its profit?
steps: A fixed cost doesn't change MC or MR, so $Q = 8$ and $P = \$12$ stay the same.

blocks.html: Because a monopoly sets its price from the demand curve, it has no supply curve of the usual kind: the quantity it offers at a given price depends on the whole shape of demand, not on the price alone.

Reading the price off the MC or MR curve at the MR = MC quantity. At 8 units, MR and MC are both \$4, but buyers will pay \$12 for 8 units, and the monopoly charges what buyers will pay. Check: the price must be a point on the demand curve.

sources.name: OpenStax Principles of Microeconomics 3e, 9.2 How a Profit-Maximizing Monopoly Chooses Output and Price
MIT OpenCourseWare 14.01 Principles of Microeconomics (scope and sequence)

blocks.html: Compare the monopoly outcome (The Monopolist's Price and Output) with what a competitive market would do with the same costs. The comparison uses allocative efficiency, $P = MC$, from Allocative and Productive Efficiency.

A monopoly produces less and charges more than a competitive market would: $P > MC$ at its output. The units between the monopoly quantity and the competitive quantity are worth more to buyers than they cost to make, but they aren't produced. That lost surplus is the deadweight loss. Much of the monopoly's profit is surplus moved from consumers to the firm, which is a transfer, not a loss.

A competitive market with the same constant cost would produce until $P = MC$. The monopoly stops earlier because selling more would mean cutting its price on every unit. Consumer surplus shrinks for two reasons: buyers who still buy pay more (that part becomes the monopoly's profit), and some buyers who would have bought at the competitive price don't buy at all (that part is lost to everyone).

blocks.name: ec-monopoly
blocks.cap: Blue: consumer surplus under monopoly. Gold: profit, most of which used to be consumer surplus. Hatched: the deadweight loss between 8 and 16 units.

blocks.title: Measure the deadweight loss
blocks.q: Demand is $P = 20 - Q$ and MC is a constant \$4. Find the competitive outcome, the monopoly outcome and the deadweight loss.
steps: Competitive: $P = MC = \$4$, so $Q = 16$.
Monopoly (from the last lesson): $Q = 8$, $P = \$12$.
blocks.a: Competition: 16 units at \$4. Monopoly: 8 at \$12. DWL \$32.

blocks.title: Where did consumer surplus go?
blocks.q: In the same market, compare consumer surplus under competition with the monopoly outcome.
steps: Competition: $CS = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 16 \times (20 - 4) = \$128$.
Monopoly: $CS = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 8 \times (20 - 12) = \$32$; profit $= \$64$; DWL $= \$32$.
$\$32 + \$64 + \$32 = \$128$: the old consumer surplus is split among consumers, the firm and nobody.

blocks.html: Counting the monopolist's extra profit as the deadweight loss. The profit rectangle is a transfer from buyers to the firm; society as a whole loses only the triangle. Check: an area someone receives (consumers, the firm, the government) is not deadweight loss.

sources.name: OpenStax Principles of Microeconomics 3e, 9.2 How a Profit-Maximizing Monopoly Chooses Output and Price
MIT OpenCourseWare 14.01 Principles of Microeconomics (scope and sequence)

blocks.html: Some industries are monopolies because one firm really is cheapest: economies of scale (Economies and Diseconomies of Scale) run across the whole market. Breaking them up would raise costs, but leaving them alone brings the deadweight loss of Monopoly and Deadweight Loss. Regulators look for a middle path.

A natural monopoly has average total cost falling over the whole range of market demand, usually because of a big fixed cost. Two common price rules: $P = MC$ is allocatively efficient but, since MC is below ATC, the firm loses money and needs a subsidy; $P = ATC$ (average-cost pricing) lets the firm break even with a small deadweight loss.

When average cost is falling, each extra unit costs less than the average so far: $MC < ATC$. So a price equal to MC is below the cost per unit, and the firm loses $(ATC - MC) \times Q$, which with a constant MC is exactly its fixed cost. Setting the price at ATC covers every cost, including a normal return, so the firm can stay in business without a subsidy, at the cost of producing a bit less than the efficient amount.

blocks.name: ec-monopoly
blocks.cap: Average total cost falls across the whole market. Try each regulation: with $P = MC$ the firm needs a subsidy; with $P = ATC$ it breaks even.

blocks.title: Unregulated, and P = MC
blocks.q: A water utility faces demand $P = 20 - Q$, has a constant marginal cost of \$4 and a fixed cost of \$48. Find its outcome unregulated and under a $P = MC$ rule.
steps: Unregulated: $MR = 20 - 2Q = 4$ gives $Q = 8$ and $P = \$12$; profit $= (12 - 4)(8) - 48 = \$16$.
At \$4 the price covers each unit's marginal cost but none of the \$48 fixed cost: a loss of \$48, which a subsidy would have to cover.
blocks.a: Unregulated: 8 units at \$12. $P = MC$: 16 units at \$4, losing \$48.

blocks.title: Average-cost pricing
blocks.q: For the same utility, find the price and quantity under a $P = ATC$ rule.
steps: $ATC = \dfrac{48}{Q} + 4$. Set it equal to demand: $20 - Q = \dfrac{48}{Q} + 4$.
Multiply by $Q$ and rearrange: $Q^2 - 16Q + 48 = 0$, so $(Q - 4)(Q - 12) = 0$.
Take the larger root, $Q = 12$ (more output at a lower price): $P = 20 - 12 = \$8$, and $ATC = 48/12 + 4 = \$8$. Zero economic profit.
blocks.a: 12 units at \$8: the firm breaks even.

blocks.html: Expecting a $P = MC$ rule to let the firm break even. With average cost falling, MC is below ATC, so price equal to MC can't cover the average cost. Check: compare MC and ATC at the regulated quantity; if MC is lower, the firm loses $(ATC - MC) \times Q$.

Real regulators also worry that a firm guaranteed to cover its costs has little reason to cut them. Rules that cap prices for several years at a time try to keep that incentive; which approach works best is debated.

blocks.html: The single-price monopoly in Monopoly and Deadweight Loss leaves sales on the table: some buyers would pay more than the price, and some would buy at a lower price. A seller who can charge different prices to different buyers can capture some of that.

Price discrimination is charging different buyers different prices for the same good, for reasons not based on cost. It needs three things: market power, a way to sort buyers by willingness to pay, and a way to prevent resale. With perfect price discrimination, each buyer pays their full willingness to pay: output rises to the competitive level, consumer surplus goes to zero and the deadweight loss disappears. With separate groups, the group with less elastic demand pays more.

With one price, the seller trades off selling more against cutting the price for everyone. If it can sort buyers, cutting the price for one group doesn't lower it for the others, so marginal revenue is higher and it sells more. In each group it sets $MR = MC$; the group with fewer alternatives (less elastic demand) gets the higher price. Resale must be blocked, or low-price buyers would resell to high-price buyers.

blocks.name: ec-monopoly
blocks.cap: Two groups with a shared marginal cost of \$2. Each gets its own MR = MC quantity; the group with less elastic demand pays more.

blocks.title: Two groups of moviegoers
blocks.q: A theater's marginal cost per seat is \$2. Adults' demand is $P = 14 - Q$; students' is $P = 8 - Q$ (Q in dozens of tickets). Students must show an ID. What price does each group pay?
steps: Adults: $MR = 14 - 2Q = 2$, so $Q = 6$ and $P = \$8$.
Students: $MR = 8 - 2Q = 2$, so $Q = 3$ and $P = \$5$.
The ID check sorts buyers and stops resale; students, with lower willingness to pay and more alternatives, pay less.

blocks.title: Perfect price discrimination
blocks.q: A seller faces demand $P = 20 - Q$ with a constant MC of \$4 and can charge each buyer exactly their willingness to pay. How much does it sell, and what is its profit?
steps: Each extra sale doesn't lower any other price, so $MR = P$: sell until $P = MC$, which is 16 units.
Profit is the whole area between demand and MC: $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 16 \times (20 - 4) = \$128$.
Consumer surplus is 0 and so is the deadweight loss: efficient, but every gain goes to the seller.

blocks.html: Calling any price difference discrimination. A plane seat booked a year ahead and one booked the day before may cost different amounts to provide, and a delivered pizza costs more to make than one picked up. Check the three conditions too: without a way to stop resale, discrimination falls apart.

blocks.html: Most restaurants, hair salons and clothing brands are neither price takers nor monopolies. Each has a slightly different product, so it faces a downward-sloping demand curve and picks a price as a monopoly does (The Monopolist's Price and Output), but anyone can open a new one, as in the competitive industries of Allocative and Productive Efficiency.

Monopolistic competition: many firms, differentiated products and free entry. In the short run each firm sets $MR = MC$ and can earn a profit. In the long run, entry pulls each firm's demand curve left until it just touches ATC: zero economic profit, with $P = ATC$ but $P > MC$, and output below the minimum of ATC (excess capacity).

Profits at the coffee shops in a neighborhood attract new coffee shops. Each newcomer takes some customers from the others, shifting each firm's demand curve left. That continues until no firm can earn more than a normal profit. At that point the demand curve is tangent to ATC: the best the firm can do is break even. Since the demand curve slopes down, the tangency happens on the falling part of ATC, so each firm produces less than the output that would minimize its average cost.

blocks.name: ec-monopoly
blocks.cap: Long run: the firm's demand curve has shifted in until it just touches ATC. Profit is zero, the price is above MC, and output is below the bottom of ATC (excess capacity).

blocks.title: Short run
blocks.q: A bakery with a popular new bread faces demand $P = 14 - Q$ (Q in loaves a day), has a marginal cost of \$4 and, at its chosen output, an ATC of \$7. Find its quantity, price and daily profit.
blocks.a: 5 loaves at \$9 each; profit \$10 a day.

blocks.title: Long run
blocks.q: New bakeries open nearby with similar breads. What happens to this bakery's demand curve, price and profit over time?
steps: Its customers have more substitutes: its demand curve shifts left (and becomes more elastic).
Entry continues until demand just touches ATC: economic profit falls to zero.
The price still exceeds MC, so it is not allocatively efficient, and it produces short of minimum ATC.
blocks.a: Demand shifts left until profit is zero.

blocks.html: Expecting long-run profits, as for a monopoly. A monopoly is protected by barriers to entry; a monopolistic competitor isn't, so new rivals keep arriving until profits are gone. Check: ask "can new firms enter?" If yes, long-run economic profit is zero.

Is the excess capacity waste? Partly, but it buys variety: more styles, locations and flavors than a perfectly competitive market of identical products would offer. How to weigh the two is a matter of judgment.

blocks.html: When an industry has only a few firms (an oligopoly), each firm's best choice depends on what the others do. A monopoly (Monopoly and Barriers to Entry) has no rivals to watch; an oligopolist does. Game theory is the tool for that. Try it in the Game Theory course's Dominance and the Prisoner's Dilemma chapter, where you can play these games against bots.

A game has players, strategies and payoffs. A payoff matrix lists one cell for each pair of strategies, with the row player's payoff first: (row, column). A player has a dominant strategy if one strategy gives them a higher payoff than their other strategies whatever the other player does.

To check for a dominant strategy, put yourself in one player's shoes and compare only that player's own payoffs. For the row player: fix a column (one choice by the other player), compare the row player's payoffs going down that column, and see which row is better. Repeat for the other column. If the same row wins both times, it's dominant. Comparing my payoff with yours answers a different question, "who does better?", which doesn't matter to my choice.

blocks.name: ec-payoff
blocks.cap: Two firms in a cartel each choose to keep the agreement or cheat. Tap each player's better payoff for each choice of the other player, then press Check.

blocks.title: Find the dominant strategy
blocks.q: Two gas stations choose prices. If both charge High, each earns \$500. If both charge Low, each earns \$300. If one charges Low and the other High, the low-price station earns \$700 and the other \$100. Does Station A (rows) have a dominant strategy?
steps: If B charges High: A earns \$500 with High and \$700 with Low. Low is better.
If B charges Low: A earns \$100 with High and \$300 with Low. Low is better.
Low is better either way: Low is A's dominant strategy (and, by symmetry, B's).

blocks.title: Only one player has one
blocks.q: Payoffs (A, B): A Up/B Left (4, 3), A Up/B Right (2, 1), A Down/B Left (3, 0), A Down/B Right (1, 2). Who has a dominant strategy?
steps: A: against Left, Up gives 4 vs 3; against Right, Up gives 2 vs 1. Up is dominant.
B: against Up, Left gives 3 vs 1; against Down, Left gives 0 vs 2. B's best choice depends on A: no dominant strategy.
B can still reason: A will play Up, so B should play Left.

blocks.html: Comparing payoffs across players ("my 5 is more than your 3") instead of comparing one player's own payoffs across that player's choices. Check: when deciding for the row player, look only at first numbers, and only down a column; for the column player, look only at second numbers, across a row.

blocks.html: Many games have no dominant strategy (Payoff Matrices and Dominant Strategies). We still need a way to predict what happens. Practice the idea in the Game Theory course's Nash Equilibrium chapter.

A Nash equilibrium is a pair of strategies in which each player's choice is a best response to the other's: no player can do better by changing their own strategy alone. To find one, mark each player's best response to every choice of the other; a cell where both payoffs are marked is a Nash equilibrium. A game can have one, several or none (in pure strategies).

At a Nash equilibrium, nobody has regrets given what the others did, so there is no pull to move. In a prisoner's dilemma, each player has a dominant strategy to defect, so (defect, defect) is the Nash equilibrium, even though both would be better off cooperating. That explains why cartels are hard to keep together: each member gains by cheating on the agreement, whatever the others do.

blocks.name: ec-payoff
blocks.cap: A prisoner's dilemma. Mark each player's best responses, then Check: the only cell with both payoffs marked is the Nash equilibrium, and it's worse for both than the cell they would agree on.

blocks.title: A cartel breaks down
blocks.q: Two firms agree to keep output low. Payoffs (A, B) in millions: both Keep (10, 10); A Cheats and B Keeps (14, 4); A Keeps and B Cheats (4, 14); both Cheat (6, 6). Find the Nash equilibrium.
steps: A's best responses: against Keep, Cheat (14 > 10); against Cheat, Cheat (6 > 4).
B's best responses are the same by symmetry.
Only (Cheat, Cheat) has both payoffs marked: the Nash equilibrium, at 6 each, worse than the 10 each from keeping the deal.

blocks.title: Two equilibria
blocks.q: Two friends pick a café without talking. Both at Café A: (3, 3); both at Café B: (2, 2); different cafés: (0, 0). Find the Nash equilibria.
steps: If the other goes to A, your best response is A (3 > 0); if the other goes to B, it's B (2 > 0).
Both (A, A) and (B, B) are Nash equilibria: neither friend wants to switch alone.

blocks.html: Thinking a Nash equilibrium must be the best outcome for both players. It's only stable: no one can gain by changing alone. In a prisoner's dilemma, both would gain by changing together, but neither can trust the other to. Check a candidate cell by asking each player in turn: "holding the other fixed, would you switch?"

Repeated play changes things: firms that meet again and again can sometimes keep cooperating, because cheating today invites punishment tomorrow. That is the subject of the Game Theory course's repeated games chapter.

blocks.html: Firms buy labor the way they make output: one more unit at a time (Profit-Maximizing Output: MR = MC). What a worker is worth to the firm depends on how much the worker adds to output, marginal product from Short-Run Production, and what that output sells for.

The marginal revenue product of labor is the extra revenue from one more worker: $$MRP = MP \times MR,$$ which is $MP \times P$ when the firm sells its output in a competitive market. A firm hires workers as long as $MRP \ge$ the wage, and stops where $MRP = W$. The MRP curve is the firm's demand curve for labor.

A new worker adds MP units of output, and each sells for P (or brings in MR), so the worker adds $MP \times P$ to revenue. The worker costs the wage. If the worker brings in more than the wage, hiring adds to profit; if less, it subtracts. Because marginal product eventually falls, MRP falls too, so the firm hires up to the point where the last worker's MRP just covers the wage. That's why labor demand is a derived demand: it comes from the demand for what the workers make.

If the firm has market power where it sells, it must cut its price to sell more, so it uses $MRP = MP \times MR$, which is smaller than $MP \times P$.

blocks.html: A labor market has a demand curve (built from MRP, Marginal Revenue Product and Hiring) and a supply curve (people's willingness to work). Shifts work exactly as in When One Curve Shifts, with the wage as the price.

Labor demand shifts when the price of (or demand for) the product changes, when productivity changes, or when the prices of other inputs change (a cheaper substitute input lowers labor demand; a cheaper complementary input raises it). Labor supply shifts with the number of workers, people's preferences and the training or licenses required, and pay in other jobs. A change in the wage itself is a movement along both curves.

Labor demand is MRP, which is MP times the product's price, so anything that changes either moves the whole curve: a rise in the price of bread raises every baker's MRP. Supply comes from people choosing among jobs and other uses of time. If pay rises in a different occupation, some workers move there, so supply to this one falls at every wage. And as always, the wage in this market is on the axis, so a wage change is a movement, not a shift.

blocks.name: ec-factor
blocks.cap: Press the buttons: each event shifts one curve, and the new equilibrium shows what happens to the wage and employment.

blocks.title: Two events for bakers
blocks.q: What happens to bakers' wages and employment? (a) Demand for bread rises, raising its price. (b) A new law requires a two-year baking license.
steps: (a) Bakers' MRP rises: labor demand shifts right. Wage up, employment up.
(b) Fewer people can enter: labor supply shifts left. Wage up, employment down.
blocks.a: (a) wage and employment rise; (b) wage rises, employment falls.

blocks.title: A substitute input
blocks.q: Self-checkout machines get much cheaper. What happens to the demand for cashiers?
steps: Machines and cashiers do the same job: they are substitute inputs.
Cheaper machines lead stores to use more machines and fewer cashiers at every wage: labor demand shifts left.

blocks.html: Shifting labor demand when the wage changes, or forgetting that labor demand is derived from demand for the product. A higher wage moves firms up along their demand curve. Check: is the wage the thing that changed? Then it's a movement. Did something change MP or the product's price? Then demand shifts.

blocks.html: Firms use more than one input. Choosing the mix is the same problem as the shopper's in Marginal Utility per Dollar: get the most for each dollar. Here the "utility" is output, and the inputs are labor and capital, valued by the MRP idea of Marginal Revenue Product and Hiring.

The least-cost rule: a firm produces any given output at the lowest cost when the last dollar spent on each input adds the same output, $$\frac{MP_L}{w} = \frac{MP_K}{r},$$ where $w$ is the wage and $r$ is the rental price of capital. The profit-maximizing rule adds that each input's MRP equals its price: $MRP_L = w$ and $MRP_K = r$.

If the last dollar on labor adds 3 units and the last dollar on machines adds 2, move a dollar from machines to labor: output rises by about 1 unit at no extra cost. Keep moving dollars until the two ratios are equal. Least cost doesn't guarantee the best scale, though: a firm could make the wrong amount cheaply. Profit maximization also needs each input hired until its MRP equals its price, which makes both ratios $MRP/\text{price}$ equal 1.

blocks.name: ec-factor
blocks.cap: Step through spending a budget: each step buys the input with the higher marginal product per dollar, until the budget is spent and the ratios are about equal.

blocks.title: Which input to add?
blocks.q: A factory's last worker adds 20 units a day and costs \$100; its last machine adds 30 units and costs \$200 a day to rent. Is it using the least-cost mix?
steps: Labor: $20 \div 100 = 0.2$ units per dollar. Capital: $30 \div 200 = 0.15$ units per dollar.
A dollar does more on labor, so shift spending toward labor and away from machines.
As it hires more workers, $MP_L$ falls; with fewer machines, $MP_K$ rises, until the ratios meet.
blocks.a: No: use more labor and less capital.

blocks.title: Profit maximizing as well
blocks.q: Product price \$2. At the current mix, $MP_L = 15$ with $w = \$30$, and $MP_K = 40$ with $r = \$80$. Is the firm at the least-cost mix? Is it maximizing profit?
steps: $MP_L/w = 15/30 = 0.5$ and $MP_K/r = 40/80 = 0.5$: equal, so it's the least-cost mix.
$MRP_L = 15 \times 2 = \$30 = w$ and $MRP_K = 40 \times 2 = \$80 = r$: both equal their prices.

blocks.html: Hiring more of the input with the higher marginal product without dividing by its price. A machine that adds 30 units beats a worker who adds 20, but not if the machine costs twice as much. Check: always compare $MP \div \text{price}$.

blocks.html: A monopsony is a single buyer, the mirror image of a monopoly. A monopoly must cut its price to sell more (Why Marginal Revenue Is Below Price); a monopsony employer must raise its wage to hire more. Instead of the shifting curves of Shifts in Labor Demand and Supply, it chooses a point on the labor supply curve.

To hire one more worker, a monopsonist must pay a higher wage to all its workers, so the marginal factor cost (MFC, also called marginal resource cost) is above the wage. It hires where $MRP = MFC$, then pays the wage on the supply curve at that number of workers. The result: fewer workers and a lower wage than a competitive labor market. With linear supply $w = w_0 + sL$, $MFC = w_0 + 2sL$.

Suppose 10 workers would work for \$15 an hour, but an 11th needs \$16. Hiring the 11th costs \$16 for that worker plus \$1 more for each of the other 10: \$26 in all. That's the MFC. Since it's above the wage, the employer stops hiring earlier than a competitive employer would, and the wage only has to be high enough to attract that smaller number of workers. In this model, a minimum wage set between the monopsony wage and the competitive wage makes the MFC flat up to the supply curve and can raise employment.

blocks.name: ec-factor
blocks.cap: MRP meets MFC at the hiring point; the dotted line drops to the supply curve for the wage. Turn on the minimum wage to see employment rise in the model.

blocks.title: A one-company town
blocks.q: Labor supply is $w = 5 + L$ (dollars an hour), and workers' MRP is $35 - L$. Find the monopsony employment and wage, and compare with a competitive market.
steps: $MFC = 5 + 2L$ (twice the slope of supply).
Wage from supply: $w = 5 + 10 = \$15$.
Competitive: $35 - L = 5 + L$ gives $L = 15$ and $w = \$20$. The monopsony hires 5 fewer and pays \$5 less.

blocks.title: MFC from a supply schedule
blocks.q: An employer can hire 3 workers at \$12 an hour or 4 at \$13. What is the marginal factor cost of the 4th worker?
steps: Labor cost with 3: $3 \times \$12 = \$36$. With 4: $4 \times \$13 = \$52$.
$MFC = \$52 - \$36 = \$16$, more than the \$13 wage.

blocks.html: Reading the wage from the MFC curve at the hiring point. MFC says what the last worker costs the firm; the wage is what workers need to be willing to work, which is on the supply curve. In the example, MFC at 10 workers is \$25, but the wage is \$15. Check: the wage must be a point on the labor supply curve.

Economists agree on this model's logic. How much monopsony power real employers have, and so what a particular minimum wage does to employment, is studied and debated; the evidence differs across places, industries and the size of the increase.

blocks.html: A competitive market maximizes total surplus (Total Surplus and Deadweight Loss) when everyone affected is a buyer or a seller. When a cost falls on someone outside the deal, that is no longer true.

A negative externality is a cost imposed on bystanders, such as pollution from a factory or noise from a highway. The marginal social cost is $MSC = MPC + MEC$: the private cost (supply) plus the marginal external cost. The market produces where demand meets private supply, more than the efficient quantity, where demand (marginal social benefit) meets MSC. The deadweight loss is the triangle between MSC and demand from the efficient quantity out to the market quantity.

Sellers decide how much to make by comparing price with their own costs. The harm to neighbors doesn't show up in their costs, so they act as if it were zero. For units past the efficient quantity, the true cost to society (private cost plus the harm) is higher than what buyers would pay; producing them destroys surplus. That's the deadweight loss, and it sits beyond the efficient quantity, because the problem is too much, not too little.

blocks.name: ec-externality
blocks.cap: Private supply understates the cost to society by the marginal external cost. The market makes too much; the hatched triangle is the deadweight loss.

blocks.title: Too much of a polluting good
blocks.q: Demand for a chemical is $P = 20 - Q$. The private marginal cost is $MPC = 2 + Q$, and each unit causes \$4 of harm downstream. Find the market quantity, the efficient quantity and the deadweight loss.
steps: Market: $20 - Q = 2 + Q$, so $Q_m = 9$.
Social cost: $MSC = 2 + Q + 4 = 6 + Q$. Efficient: $20 - Q = 6 + Q$, so $Q_e = 7$.
At $Q_m = 9$ the gap between MSC and demand is $(6 + 9) - (20 - 9) = 4$.
$DWL = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 4 \times (9 - 7) = \$4$.

blocks.title: Who bears the cost?
blocks.q: In the example, what are the total external costs at the market quantity?
steps: Each unit causes \$4 of harm, and 9 units are made.
External cost: $9 \times \$4 = \$36$, borne by people downstream who are not part of the trade.

blocks.html: Putting the deadweight loss on the wrong side of the efficient quantity, or thinking the market makes too little of a good that pollutes. Ignoring a cost makes production look cheaper than it is, so the market makes too much. Check: the market quantity is where the lower, private curve crosses demand, which is to the right of where the higher, social curve does.

blocks.html: Externalities can be good too. The logic of Negative Externalities runs in reverse when a benefit spills onto bystanders.

A positive externality is a benefit to bystanders: a flu shot protects the people around you, and research by one firm helps others. When the benefit comes from using the good, the marginal social benefit is $MSB = MPB + MEB$, a curve above demand. The market produces where demand (private benefit) meets supply, less than the efficient quantity where MSB meets supply. The deadweight loss is the triangle between MSB and supply, from the market quantity to the efficient quantity.

Buyers compare the price with their own benefit. The protection their flu shot gives coworkers doesn't enter that decision, so they buy as if it were zero. Units between the market quantity and the efficient quantity are worth more to society (buyer plus bystanders) than they cost to make, but no one buys them. When the spillover comes from producing a good, as when a beekeeper's bees pollinate nearby orchards, the external benefit lowers the social cost instead: the social cost curve lies below supply.

blocks.name: ec-externality
blocks.cap: The marginal social benefit curve sits above demand. The market makes too little; the hatched triangle is the deadweight loss.

blocks.title: Flu shots
blocks.q: At a clinic, private demand for flu shots is $P = 40 - Q$ (Q in shots a day), supply is $P = 10 + Q$, and each shot gives other people \$10 of protection. Find the market and efficient quantities and the deadweight loss.
steps: Market: $40 - Q = 10 + Q$, so $Q_m = 15$.
$MSB = 50 - Q$. Efficient: $50 - Q = 10 + Q$, so $Q_e = 20$.
$DWL = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 10 \times (20 - 15) = \$25$ a day.
blocks.a: Market 15, efficient 20 shots a day; DWL \$25 a day.

blocks.title: Which side?
blocks.q: A homeowner's flower garden pleases the neighbors. Where does the external benefit go on the graph of gardening?
steps: The benefit comes from the garden existing, which is the homeowner's consumption choice.
It adds to the benefit side: MSB lies above the homeowner's demand.
blocks.a: On the benefit side, above demand.

blocks.html: Drawing a benefit from consuming a good on the supply side. A flu shot's spillover comes from people using it, so it raises the social benefit curve above demand; supply doesn't change. Check: ask "does the spillover come from buying and using, or from producing?" and draw it on that side.

blocks.html: Externalities (Positive Externalities) leave the market at the wrong quantity. A per-unit tax or subsidy (Per-Unit Subsidies) can move it to the right one, and there are other tools too.

A Pigouvian tax equal to the marginal external cost at the efficient quantity makes sellers pay for the harm, so the market lands on the efficient quantity. A subsidy equal to the marginal external benefit does the same for positive externalities. Other tools: tradable permits (cap the total and let firms trade the right to pollute) and direct rules (limits or required technology). The efficient amount of pollution is usually not zero: cut pollution until the marginal benefit of cutting equals the marginal cost.

A tax of \$4 per unit on a good that causes \$4 of harm per unit shifts private supply up to the social cost curve, so the market's own crossing becomes the efficient one. Permits reach a target in a different way: firms that can cut pollution cheaply do more of the cutting and sell their spare permits to firms for which cutting is expensive. Why not cut pollution to zero? The first tons are cheap to remove and do a lot of good; the last tons may require shutting down useful production entirely. Past the point where the next ton's cleanup costs more than the harm it causes, cleaning more makes society worse off.

blocks.name: ec-externality
blocks.cap: Marginal benefit and marginal cost of cleanup. They cross below 100%: past that point, more cleanup costs more than it's worth (hatched).

blocks.title: The right tax
blocks.q: From Negative Externalities: demand $P = 20 - Q$, private cost $MPC = 2 + Q$ and \$4 of harm per unit. What tax brings the market to the efficient quantity of 7?
steps: With a tax $t$ on sellers, supply becomes $P = 2 + Q + t$.
For the market to land at 7: $20 - 7 = 2 + 7 + t$, so $t = \$4$, the marginal external cost.

blocks.title: How much cleanup?
blocks.q: The marginal benefit of cutting pollution is $MB = 90 - 0.8x$ and the marginal cost is $MC = 0.7x$ (dollars, with $x$ the percent cut). What is the efficient percent?
steps: Cutting more than 60% costs more per percent than the damage it prevents.

blocks.html: Thinking the efficient amount of pollution is zero. Zero pollution would mean giving up many useful things whose benefits exceed the harm. The efficient amount is where the marginal benefit of cutting equals the marginal cost of cutting. Check: compare the cost of the last unit of cleanup with the damage it prevents.

Economists broadly favor pricing tools (taxes and tradable permits) for reaching a pollution target at the lowest cost. How high to set the price or the cap depends on how much the harm is valued, which involves both science and judgment, and is debated.

blocks.html: Markets handle some goods well and others poorly. Two questions, both about the scarce resources from Scarcity and the Factors of Production, sort goods into four kinds.

A good is excludable if people who don't pay can be kept from using it. It is rival if one person's use leaves less for others. Private goods are rival and excludable (a sandwich). Club goods are excludable but not rival (a streaming service). Common resources are rival but not excludable (fish in the open ocean). Public goods are neither (national defense).

Markets work best for private goods: sellers can charge, and each unit goes to one buyer. Without excludability, people can use a good without paying, so sellers struggle to cover costs (the subject of Public Goods and Free Riders). Without rivalry, keeping someone out wastes something that would cost nothing to share. Common resources get overused, because each user takes what they want and ignores that it leaves less for everyone else.

blocks.title: Sort three goods
blocks.q: Classify: (a) a toll road with little traffic; (b) a pond where anyone may fish; (c) a fireworks show seen across town.

(c) Anyone in town can see it, and one viewer doesn't reduce another's view: a public good.

blocks.html: Calling anything the government provides a public good. A public school can turn students away and has limited seats, so it is excludable and largely rival; governments provide it for other reasons. National defense, by contrast, is both nonrival and nonexcludable. Check: answer the two questions (can nonpayers be kept out? does one person's use leave less?) before naming the type.

blocks.html: Public goods are nonrival and nonexcludable (Rival and Excludable Goods), and like other goods with spillovers (Positive Externalities), markets tend to provide too little of them. The reason is a game, played out in the Game Theory course's Dominance and the Prisoner's Dilemma chapter, where a public-goods game unravels.

Because no one can be kept from using a public good, each person can free ride: enjoy it without paying. So private sellers can't collect enough to cover the cost, and markets supply too little. A public good is worth providing when the sum of everyone's benefits is at least its cost; for each extra unit, compare the sum of the marginal benefits with the marginal cost.

Each person reasons: "If others pay, I get it free; if they don't, my small payment won't buy it alone." Not paying is a dominant strategy, as in a prisoner's dilemma, so the good may not get provided even when everyone would be better off if all paid. And because one person's use doesn't reduce anyone else's, the value of a unit is everyone's benefit added together, not one person's. That's why taxes, which everyone pays, often fund public goods.

blocks.name: ec-payoff
blocks.cap: Two neighbors each choose whether to chip in for a shared project. Mark the best responses: not contributing is each one's dominant strategy, even though both gain if both contribute.

blocks.title: A streetlight
blocks.q: A streetlight costs \$75. Three neighbors value it at \$40, \$30 and \$20. Should it be built? Will any one neighbor buy it alone?
steps: Total benefit: $\$40 + \$30 + \$20 = \$90 > \$75$: it's worth building.
No single neighbor values it at \$75 or more, so none buys it alone.
And each hopes the others pay: a free-rider problem. Splitting the cost by a rule, such as a tax of \$25 each, gets it built.
blocks.a: Yes, it should be built (\$90 > \$75), but no one will buy it alone.

blocks.title: How many units?
blocks.q: A town is deciding how many benches to put in its park. For benches 1 to 4, the marginal benefit to Group A is \$40, \$30, \$20 and \$10, and to Group B \$35, \$25, \$15 and \$5. Each bench costs \$50. How many should it build?
steps: Everyone can use every bench, so a bench's value is the sum of both groups' benefits.
Add vertically for each bench: \$75, \$55, \$35, \$15.
Benches 1 and 2 are worth more than \$50; bench 3 (\$35) isn't. Build 2.

blocks.html: Comparing the cost with one person's benefit instead of the sum of everyone's. By that test the streetlight (worth at most \$40 to any one neighbor) would fail, though it's worth \$90 to the street. Check: for a public good, add the benefits of everyone who uses it.

blocks.html: Labor markets set wages (Shifts in Labor Demand and Supply), and wages are most of most people's income. How evenly is income shared? Economists summarize it with shares of a whole, the idea from Percent Means per 100.

Line up households from lowest income to highest and split them into five equal groups (quintiles). The Lorenz curve plots the cumulative share of households against the cumulative share of income. Perfect equality is the diagonal line. The Gini coefficient is $A/(A + B)$, where $A$ is the area between the diagonal and the Lorenz curve and $B$ is the area under the curve: 0 means perfect equality; values near 1 mean extreme inequality.

With perfect equality, the bottom 20% of households would have 20% of income, the bottom 40% would have 40%, and so on: the diagonal. Any real distribution gives the bottom groups less than their share, so the curve sags below the diagonal. The more it sags, the bigger area $A$ and the larger the Gini. Because $A + B$ is the whole triangle under the diagonal (area $\tfrac{1}{2}$), $\text{Gini} = A / \tfrac{1}{2} = 1 - 2B$.

blocks.name: ec-lorenz

blocks.title: Cumulative shares
blocks.q: Income shares by quintile, poorest first: 4%, 9%, 15%, 23%, 49%. What share of income goes to the bottom 60%?
steps: Add the first three: $4\% + 9\% + 15\% = 28\%$.
So the bottom 60% of households get 28% of income; the top 20% alone get 49%.

blocks.title: A Gini from five points
blocks.q: Using the same shares, estimate the Gini coefficient with trapezoids.

blocks.html: Reading a Lorenz curve farther from the diagonal as more equal, or a higher Gini as more equal. The diagonal is equality, so distance from it measures inequality, and the Gini grows with that distance. Check: a Gini of 0 is the diagonal itself.

For current U.S. figures, use the Census Bureau's income tables; numbers vary by year and by how income is measured (before or after taxes and transfers). What causes inequality and how much to reduce it are debated, and the answers mix evidence with values.
